# وإنما جعلنا البعد

من عند نصف النهار لأن التعديل للميلاد به أسهل من العمل بالآفاق وساعات النهار
الأطول لعرض بيت المقدس أربع عشرة ساعة وشئ فلا يستقيم عمل اليهود
بالساعات الزمانية إلا أن يكون الاجتماع لرأس تشري واقعاً مع الاعتدال
الخريفي وليس يقع معه أبداً بل يتقدمه ويتأخر عنه مقداراً كثيراً كما بينا
فيما تقدم فإذا استخرجنا وقت الاجتماع بالحساب الذي أورده اليهود في الجدول
الذي حللناه على رأيهم ترقينا من ذلك إلى علم أول السنة ومعرفة كيفيتها
في النقصان والاعتدال والتمام وقد تقدمت لنا المعرفة بما هي بسيطة أم كبيسة
فنطلب في جدول الحدود مدة من أيام الأسبوع يتضمن حدّاها طرفاها الوقت
الذي خرج لنا الاجتماع فيه في جانب الكبوس إن كانت كبوساً وفي جانب البسائط إن
كانت بسيطة فإذا وجدناه ألفينا بحذائه أول السنة من الأسبوع وكيفيتها
وإذا علمنا أول السنة وكيفيتها وركبنا تلك الكيفية مع البساطة
أو الكبوس عرفنا من ذلك مضي أول السنة المقبلة

(In this our calculation of the conjunction) we have used noon as terminus a quo for no other reason but this, that we may more easily find the equation for the moled by this method than by using the horizons (i.e. reckoning from sunset, as the Jews do).
The hours of the longest day for the latitude of Jerusalem are 13h. plus a fraction. Therefore the calculation of the Jews by ὧραι καιρικαί is incorrect, except in case the conjunction at the beginning of Tishri should coincide with the autumnal equinox. This, however, never happens. On the contrary, the conjunction at the beginning of Tishri always either precedes or follows the autumnal equinox by a considerable space of time, as we have explained heretofore.
Relation between the beginning of the Year and its Character. — If we, now, make out the time of the conjunction by the traditional calculation of the Jews, or by means of the table which we have constructed according to their theory, we arrive at the knowledge of the beginning of the year and of its character, whether it be imperfect, intermediate, or perfect, whilst we have already previously learnt how to know whether the year be a common or a leap year. Thereupon we look in the Table of Limits for a space of time in the week within the limits of which the conjunction as found by our calculation falls. If the year be a leap year, we look into the column of leap years; if it be a common year, we look into the column of common years. Having made out this, we find opposite the indication of the week-day on which the year commences, and of the quality of the year. Once knowing the beginning of the year (its precise date in the week) and its quality, and combining with it our knowledge as to whether the year is a common or a leap year, we come to know the beginning of the next following year.
Here follows the Table of the Limits:—

# We Have Established the Distance

From the meridian because the adjustment for the birth <note>referring to the calculation of the new moon or birth of the month</note> is easier with it than by working with horizons. The longest daylight hours for the latitude of Jerusalem <note>original: "Bayt al-Maqdis"</note> are fourteen hours and some fraction. The Jewish practice of using seasonal hours <note>term: "al-sa‘at al-zamaniyya" gloss: hours of varying length based on the duration of daylight</note> is only correct if the conjunction for the beginning of Tishrei <note>the first month of the civil year</note> occurs exactly with the autumnal equinox. However, it never occurs exactly then, but rather precedes or follows it by a significant amount as we have demonstrated previously. 

When we extract the time of the conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table which we analyzed according to their view, we then proceed to determine the start of the year and its quality—whether it is deficient, intermediate, or complete. We already have the knowledge of whether the year is an ordinary year <note>term: "basita" gloss: a year of twelve months</note> or a leap year <note>term: "kabisa" gloss: an intercalary year of thirteen months</note>. 

We then search the Table of Limits for a duration of weekdays whose boundaries contain the time we calculated for the conjunction. We look in the section for leap years if it is a leap year, or in the section for ordinary years if it is an ordinary year. When we find it, we will find alongside it the first day of the year in the week and its specific quality. Once we know the start of the year and its quality, and combine that quality with its status as an ordinary or leap year, we can determine the arrival of the following year's beginning.

# This is the Table of Limits

# The Reason We Established the Distance

We have established the distance from the point of midday <note>the meridian</note> because calculating the adjustment for a birth <note>an astrological natal chart</note> is easier by this method than by working with horizons. Furthermore, the longest daylight hours for the latitude of Jerusalem are fourteen hours and some fraction. The Jewish method of calculation using seasonal hours <note>hours of varying length depending on the time of year</note> does not function correctly unless the conjunction <term>molad</term> <gloss>the calculated time of the new moon</gloss> for the beginning of the month of Tishrei occurs exactly at the autumnal equinox. This never actually happens; rather, it precedes or follows the equinox by a significant amount, as we have demonstrated previously. 

Once we have extracted the time of the conjunction using the calculations provided by the Jews in the table we analyzed according to their views, we can then proceed to determine the start of the year. We can also identify the nature of the year: whether it is deficient, regular, or complete. We will have already determined whether the year is common <term>basita</term> <gloss>a regular 12-month year</gloss> or an intercalary <term>kabisa</term> <gloss>a 13-month leap year</gloss>.

We then consult the Table of Limits <note>the boundaries for determining the New Year</note> for a period of days of the week whose two endpoints encompass the time we calculated for the conjunction. We look in the column for intercalary years if it is a leap year, or in the column for common years if it is a regular year. When we find the correct entry, we will find alongside it the day of the week for the start of the year and its specific quality. By knowing the start of the year and its quality, and combining that quality with its status as common or intercalary, we can then determine the start of the following year.

"At the time of rein-twisting (assaulting) — for a king
"It is not proper to conquer by stealth."
Another spy began,
Saying: — "Dara prepared not such an army
"That, in the imagination, could compute it
"Those persons (officers) who are army-understanding."
Sikandar said to him: — "A sharp sword
"Makes shreds of the hide of a hundred oxen."
To the army, such an excellent reply,
From the lofty monarch, was agreeable.
Every moment, news became more ardent (instant),
That the raging dragon (Dara) had come.
When Sikandar knew that that fierce cloud
Brought forth, thunder-like, the sword's flash (of battle),
He sent (a messenger), — that an army, from every region,
Should set out to the monarch's door.
From Egypt, and Afranchiya, and Rum, and Russia,
An army, bride-like, became arrayed.
When that countless army became massed,
He sought the enumeration of the names of the renowned ones.
The general gave information that six hundred thousand
Warriors, extraordinary horsemen, were mustered.
When the business (mustering) of the army became completed,
He prepared an assembly (muster) — without wine-cup or music.
The brains (sages) of Rum sate attentive;
They made the wax (of the heart) soft, in love for the king.
Of Dara's action (in invading his kingdom) and of his strife, — the king
Urged speech, and was perturbed as to his (Dara's) action.

<meta>Sharafnāma, Nizami Ganjavi, Page 161</meta>

For the King, at the time of turning the reins,
Victory should not be sought through theft <note>meaning through deception or stealth</note>.
The researcher began once more,
Saying that Darius <note>Dara</note> has prepared so much fat <note>meaning provisions and strength</note>,
That it can be calculated in measure
By those who are experts in analyzing armies.
Alexander said to him: "One sharp sword
Can cut the fat of a hundred oxen into tiny pieces." <note>A metaphor suggesting that a single superior force can destroy a much larger, stationary mass.</note>
Such a worthy answer to the army
Came forth from the exalted Sovereign.
The news grew more heated at every moment
That a breathing dragon <note>referring to Darius</note> was approaching Rome.
When Alexander realized that that fierce cloud <note>original: "tund migh"</note> <note>Darius is compared to a storm cloud flashing with the lightning of swords.</note>
Was rarely drawing the lightning of the sword,
He sent word so that the army from every land
Would set out toward the court of the Sovereign.
From Egypt, Africa, Rome, and Russia,
An army was adorned like a bride.
When the boundless army became a vast multitude,
He requested a count of the names of the illustrious men.
The muster-master <term>Arid</term> <gloss>military official in charge of reviews and payroll</gloss> reported that three hundred thousand
Brave, solitary riders <note>elite cavalrymen</note> had come forward.
When the preparation of the army was complete,
He held a gathering outside with the cup.
The wise minds of Rome sat together;
They softened their hearts like wax for the King's seal <note>meaning they became fully submissive to his command</note>.
The King spoke of the affairs of Darius and his actions,
And reflected deeply upon his conduct.

<column-break/>

<margin>
1. Meaning one sword can mince the fat and tallow of a hundred fattened oxen. Variant: "Can pierce the hides of a hundred oxen" or "the backs of a hundred oxen."
</margin>
<margin>
2. Meaning Alexander realized that Darius is a fierce cloud who, with the roar of thunder, draws the lightning of the sword toward him.
</margin>
<margin>
3. Meaning the presenter and army scribe reported that three hundred thousand single riders <note>matchless heroes</note> were gathered. Variant: "Six hundred thousand."
</margin>
<margin>
4. Meaning by the seal of Alexander's command, they softened the wax of their hearts and became receptive to his order; soft wax accepts an impression more easily than hard wax.
</margin>

<summary>Alexander the Great responds to news of Darius's massive mobilization with a metaphor about a sharp sword and prepares his own multi-national coalition. The page describes the gathering of three hundred thousand elite troops and the king's strategic consultations.</summary>
<keywords>Alexander the Great, Darius, military mobilization, Rome, Egypt, Russia, cavalry, Sharafnama</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
When the King turned the reins <note>original: "inan taftan"</note> to depart,
One cannot find victory through theft.
Another researcher began to report,
That Dara <note>Darius III of Persia</note> has prepared such a vast army,
Which can be calculated in estimation,
By those who are experts in identifying military forces.
Alexander said to him: a single sharp blade
Can cut the fat of a hundred oxen into tiny pieces. <note>Alexander implies that a smaller, sharper force can defeat a bloated, larger army.</note>
Such a worthy answer for the army
Came forth from the exalted Sovereign.
The news became more heated at every moment,
That a roaring dragon had arrived in Rome.
When Alexander realized that the fierce cloud <note>referring to Dara's approaching army</note>
Rarely flashes the lightning of the sword without striking,
He sent word so that the army from every land
Should set out toward the gate of the Sovereign.
From Egypt, Africa, Rome, and Russia,
The army was adorned like a bride.
When the boundless army became a massive throng,
He requested a count of the names of the illustrious men.
The muster-master reported that three hundred thousand
Guerilla cavalrymen and brave champions had emerged.
When the organization of the army was complete,
He held an assembly outside with the wine-cup.
The wise minds of Rome sat together;
They softened their hearts like wax toward the King's seal.
The King spoke of the affairs of Dara and his deeds;
He discussed the matter and turned his thoughts toward him.

<column-break/>

<margin>
1. Meaning: a single sword can slice the fat and grease of a hundred fattened oxen into pieces. Other versions read: "the hide of a hundred oxen" or "the backs of a hundred oxen."
</margin>
<margin>
2. Meaning: When Alexander realized that Dara was a violent cloud drawing the lightning of his blade toward him with the roar of thunder.
</margin>
<margin>
3. Meaning: The reporter and military scribe informed him that three hundred thousand single riders had gathered. A "single rider" <term>mufrad sawar</term> refers to a peerless and unique hero. Some versions say six hundred thousand.
</margin>
<margin>
4. Meaning: Through the seal of Alexander's command, they softened the wax of their hearts and became receptive to his orders. Soft wax accepts an impression more quickly than hard wax.
</margin>

<summary>Alexander the Great responds to news of Darius's massive mobilization with a metaphor about quality over quantity, then gathers a diverse coalition of three hundred thousand troops from Egypt to Russia to prepare for the coming conflict.</summary>
<keywords>Alexander the Great, Darius, Sharafnama, military mobilization, Rome, Egypt, Russia, mufrad sawar, warfare metaphors</keywords>

The muster-master reported that three hundred thousand <margin>3. That is to say, the presenter and army-scribe reported that three hundred thousand unique riders had gathered. "Mofred-savār" (unique rider) or "yekkeh-savār" means a peerless hero. Variant reading: Six hundred thousand.</margin>
Brave and peerless riders had come forth.

He held a gathering outside with the cup <note>clarification: of wine</note>.
The wise minds of Rome sat together,
And softened the wax with the seal of the King. <margin>4. That is to say, by the seal of Alexander's command, they softened the wax of their hearts and became receptive to his order. Soft wax accepts the seal faster than hard wax.</margin>
The King spoke of the affairs of Dara
And turned his thoughts toward his <note>clarification: Darius's</note> actions.

<summary>Alexander the Great responds to reports of Darius's massive army with a metaphor about a single sword's power and subsequently musters a vast international force to face the Persian threat.</summary>

He did not seek to find victory through theft.

"Dara has prepared so much fat <note>clarification: referring to the immense size of his army</note>
That those who are experts in armies

Such a noble reply to the troops
Rose high from the exalted Monarch.
Every moment the news grew more intense
That a breathing dragon was coming toward Rome.
When Alexander knew that that fierce cloud <margin>2. That is, Alexander knew that Dara is a fierce cloud that draws the lightning of his blade toward him with the roar of thunder.</margin>
Was rarely drawing the lightning of his blade,
He sent word for the armies from every land
To set out toward the Monarch’s gate.
From Egypt, Africa, Rome, and Russia,
The army was adorned like a bride.
When the boundless army became a vast throng,
He requested the count from the rolls of the famous men.
The muster-master reported that three hundred thousand <margin>3. That is, the presenter and army scribe reported that three hundred thousand single riders had gathered. A "single rider" <term>mufrad sawār</term> <gloss>unparalleled hero</gloss> is a peerless champion. Other versions say: six hundred thousand.</margin>
Vanguard heroes and single riders had come forth.
When the preparation of the army was complete,
He held an assembly outside with the cup.
The wise minds of Rome sat together; <margin>4. That is, they softened the wax of their hearts with the seal of Alexander's command and became receptive to his order. Soft wax accepts an impression more readily than hard wax.</margin>
They softened like wax at the King’s seal.
The King spoke of Dara’s deeds and his affairs,
And reflected deeply upon his situation.

<summary>Alexander the Great responds to news of the overwhelming size of the Persian King Dara's army with a metaphor of a sharp blade cutting through fat, then musters a massive multinational force to prepare for the coming conflict.</summary>

reference_text:
[context] My heart was grieved at his miserable plight, (and) I thought it inhuman, in such a state, to irritate the poor man's wound
with reproach, and sprinkle salt thereon; I said to myself,—
Distichs.
The wretched fellow, in the extreme of intoxication,
Was not apprehensive of the day of distress.
A tree drops its blossoms and fruit profusely in spring;
In winter, as a matter of course, it remains leafless.
STORY VI.
A king made his son over to a teacher, and said, "He is thy son; educate him in the same way as a son of thine own." He replied, "I am your obedient servant." For some years he laboured hard, and exerted himself in his behoof, (but) he made no progress, while the teacher's own sons became perfect in scholarship and rhetoric. The king took the learned man to task, and censured him, saying, "Thou hast acted contrary to thy promise, and hast not fulfilled the conditions of fidelity." He replied, "It cannot be concealed from the world-adorning judgment of the lord of the earth, that education is the same, but capacities differ."
Stanza.
Although silver and gold come out of stone,
There is not silver and gold in every stone.

candidates.text:
Enduring blame and pouring salt on the wound <note>original: "ملامت کشیدن و نمک بر جراحت پاشیدن"</note>. I did not see it as wise, and said to myself:

**Poetic Fragment**
One should not be a companion to the table at the end of intoxication. Even if the locust of the hand <note>a metaphor for poverty or a reaching hand</note> scatters the gold of the trees' sustenance in the spring, in the winter it remains without leaves or fruit <note>the original implies the consequences of squandering resources</note>.

**Tale**
A king entrusted his son to a teacher <term>adīb</term> <gloss>a tutor of literature and morals</gloss>, saying, "Educate my child as you would one of your own." The teacher strove for several years, and it reached a point where his own children became accomplished in knowledge, yet the prince remained ignorant. The king summoned the wise man and rebuked him, saying, "You have broken your promise and did not fulfill the conditions." The teacher replied, "O Lord of the Earth, it is not hidden from your enlightened mind that although the education is the same, the nature of the student differs."

**Poetic Fragment**
Although silver and gold come out of stone, they are not found in every stone.

<summary>A teacher explains to a king that while education is a universal process, the inherent nature and capacity of the student determine the final result. The text uses metaphors of seasonal change and mineral extraction to illustrate the limits of instruction on different characters.</summary>
<keywords>Sa'di, Gulistan, education, nature versus nurture, pedagogy, Persian literature, moral tales</keywords>

Accepting blame and pouring salt on a wound.
I did not see any benefit in this, and I said to myself: **Poetry** A companion at the table should not become a burden at the end of a drunken revelry. When the locust of fate strips the trees bare, the tree that scattered its leaves in the spring remains naked and fruitless in the winter.

### Story
A king entrusted his son to a <term>teacher</term> <gloss>adib</gloss>, saying, "Educate my child as you have educated one of your own." The teacher labored for several years and achieved results, yet while the teacher's own sons reached the highest peaks of knowledge, the king's son remained ignorant. The King summoned the scholar and began to reprimand and rebuke him. He said, "You have broken your promise and failed to fulfill the conditions of our agreement."

The teacher replied, "O Sovereign of the face of the earth, it is not hidden from your enlightened mind that although the education is the same, the natural dispositions are different." **Poetry** Though silver and gold come out of stone, not every stone contains silver and gold.

<summary>A story illustrating that while education and training may be identical, the inherent nature or talent of the student determines the final outcome. Sa’di uses the metaphor of minerals in stones to explain why some excel while others fail despite equal effort.</summary>
<keywords>education, nature versus nurture, kingship, teaching, natural disposition, Sa'di, Gulistan</keywords>

When, on account of asininity, a tethered ass becomes violent, both his (fore-)legs will be shackled in addition.
Then the ass will say, “One tether is enough for me”; (but) in sooth do not think (that such is the case), for those two are (result) from the action of that vile creature.
In exposition of the following Hadith of Mustafa (Mohammed), on whom be peace: “Verily, the most High God created the angels and set reason in them, and He created the beasts and set lust in them, and He created the sons of Adam and set in them reason and lust; and he whose reason prevails over his lust is higher than the angels, and he whose lust prevails over his reason is lower than the beasts.”
It is related in the Hadith that the majestical God created the creatures of the world (in) three kinds.
One class (He made) entirely reason and knowledge and munificence; that is the angel: he knoweth naught but prostration in worship.
In his original nature is no concupiscence and sensuality: he is absolute light, (he is) living through (his) love of God.
Another class is devoid of knowledge, like the animal (which lives) in fatness from (eating) fodder.
It sees nothing but stable and fodder: it is heedless of (future) misery and glory (felicity).
The third (class) is Adam’s descendant and Man: half of him is of the angel and half of him is ass.
The ass-half, indeed, inclines to that which is low; the other half inclines to that which is rational.
Those two classes (the angels and the beasts) are at rest from war and combat, while this Man is (engaged) in torment (painful struggle) with two adversaries.
And, moreover, this (race of) Man, through probation, has been divided: they (all) are of human shape, but (in truth) they have become three communities (families).
One party have become submerged absolutely and, like Jesus, have attained unto the (nature of the) angel.
The form (of such a one is that of) Adam, but the reality is Gabriel: he has been delivered from anger and sensual passion and (vain) disputation.
He has been delivered from discipline and asceticism and self-mortification: you would say he was not even born of a child of Adam.
The second sort have attained unto (the nature of) asses: they have become pure anger and absolute lust.
The qualities of Gabriel were in them and departed: that house was (too) narrow, and those qualities (too) grand.
The person who is deprived of (the vital) spirit becomes dead: when his spirit is deprived of those (angelic qualities), he becomes an ass,
Because the spirit that hath not those (qualities) is vile: this word is true, and the (perfect) Sufi has said (it).
He (the man of animal nature) suffers more anxiety than the beasts, (for) he practises subtle arts in the world.
The cunning and imposture which he knows how to spin — that (cunning) is not produced by any other animal.
To weave gold-embroidered robes, to win pearls from the bottom of the sea.
The fine artifices of geometry or astronomy, and the science of medicine and philosophy —
Which are connected only with this world and have no way (of mounting) up to the Seventh Heaven —
All this is the science of building the (worldly) stable which is the pillar (basis) of the existence of (persons like) the ox and the camel.
For the sake of preserving the animal for a few days, these crazy fools have given to those (arts and sciences) the name of “mysteries.”

Since like a hobbled donkey <note>clarification: the soul</note> you are headstrong, out of donkey-ish nature,
He tied both its feet and its head.
Since the blindfolded donkey bolted and [entered] <unclear>...</unclear>
Then the donkey says, "One bond is enough for me."
Indeed, the sewing of the sack is the act of that base one.
Behold, for the donkey, a single bond at the beginning is enough.
<column-break/>
In explanation of that tradition of the Chosen One, peace be upon him: "Indeed, God Most High created the angels and placed intellect within them; and He created the beasts and placed lust within them; and He created the sons of Adam and placed within them both intellect and lust. So, he whose intellect overcomes his lust is higher than the angels, and he whose lust overcomes his intellect is lower than the beasts." The Truthful Messenger of God spoke the truth.

In the tradition, it is said that the Glorious Lord <note>original: "یزدان مجید"</note>
Created the inhabitants of the world in three kinds.
One group, in whom intellect, knowledge, and generosity prevail,
That is the angel; he knows nothing but prostration.
There is no greed or desire in his element,
Absolute light, living by the love of God.
Another group is void of knowledge,
Like animals [living] on fodder in <unclear>...</unclear>
They consider nothing but the stable and fodder;
They are ignorant of wretchedness and of honor.
This third kind is the son of Adam and human;
Half of him is a donkey, the other half inclines toward the sublime.
The donkey-half is inclined to the lowlands,
And this human is [made of] wind and contradiction.
Those two groups <note>clarification: angels and animals</note> are at peace from war and strife,
While this human is divided into three communities by the trial.
One group has become absolutely submerged <note>clarification: in God</note>,
Like Jesus, they have joined with the angels.
Delivered from anger, desire, and idle talk,
A human form, but in meaning, Gabriel.
Freed from ascetic discipline, piety, and struggle,
They have arrived [at the goal] from the lineage of humanity itself.
The other group has joined with the [beasts];
They have become pure anger and absolute lust.
That house <note>clarification: the body</note> was narrow, and that description <note>clarification: the divine attribute</note> vanished;
The Gabriel-like quality in them was [lost].
He made [it] dead, and the person who is without a soul
Is base, because of the soul that he does not possess.
He acts with a soul lower than the animals;
The deceit and trickery that he is able to weave—
The weaving of gold-embroidered garments,
Finding pearls in the depths of the sea,
With astronomy, the science of medicine, and philosophy,
He has no path to the seventh heaven.
For the pillar <note>clarification: of his knowledge</note> was the one that the ox held;
They named that "the mysteries of the universe,"
While its purpose is the preservation of the animal for a few days.
<column-break/>
He made his feet bound and [bound] his head;
He himself makes two feet into a head-bond.
His own act is [hidden] in that <unclear>...</unclear> and base one.
It is the explanation of the noble tradition:
When the Glorious Creator came to the secret,
He made the creatures evident in three kinds.
To one group He gave intellect and existence,
Who are the angels who perform prostration.
In their element, greed and desire do not exist;
They became the manifestation of the love of God.
He made one group void of knowledge;
They became entangled with animality.
Their knowledge is the stable and fodder;
They are heedless of wretchedness and lack of honor.
The third category was the human species;
They became capable of both good and evil.
Like the beasts, he has an inclination for the low;
The other half, like an angel, is of noble birth.
In humans, there is reaction between two opposites.
The human form became three communities, however:
The group joined to the ranks of angels, of angelic station,
Delivered from anger, desire, and idle talk.
Image them not as sons of Adam,
Those who are simple-hearted through piety and discipline.
The final category has the character of beasts,
Nothing but pure anger and absolute lust.
The house is narrow, that lofty description has faded;
The Gabriel-like quality has reached decline.
The person who is without a beloved first becomes dead;
The soul that is without the beloved is base and low.
The animal soul is far deeper in sorrow;
It performs every meticulous task for the world.
No other animal can act in such a way:
The gold-embroidered garment <unclear>...</unclear>
Drawing forth jewels from the depths of the sea.
Well-known philosophy, also medicine and astronomy—
There is no passage to the seventh heaven.
It pays attention to the ox and the donkey;
This attachment is worldly, from end to end.
This science of construction is tied to the manger;
The name of that fool is "the one who knows mysteries,"
Whose purpose is the preservation of the animal for a few days.

Rūmī describes how humans can ascend to angelic heights or sink below animals, noting that worldly sciences like medicine and astronomy are "animal" pursuits if they do not lead to spiritual heaven.</summary>

<keywords>Intellect, Lust, Angels, Animals, Human Nature, Jesus, Gabriel, Philosophy, Astronomy, Medicine, Spiritual Ascent</keywords>

<meta>This page contains the Persian text of Rūmī's Masnavī with an Ottoman Turkish interlinear translation and commentary in the columns. The passage focuses on the tripartite nature of creation as explained in a prophetic tradition.</meta>

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Like a stubborn donkey with its feet tied, | He tied both its feet and on the head, | Like a blindfolded donkey, it pulled its head and in, |
| Then the donkey says one binding is enough for me, | That very action is the deed of that vile one, | Verily, one binding is enough for a donkey in weeping, |

### Explanation of that Hadith of Mustafa <note>context: The Prophet Muhammad</note>, peace be upon him: "Indeed, God Almighty created the angels and placed intellect in them; He created the beasts and placed desire in them; and He created the children of Adam and placed both intellect and desire in them. He whose intellect overcomes his desire is higher than the angels, and he whose desire overcomes his intellect is lower than the beasts." The Messenger of God spoke the truth.

<column-break/>

God the Glorious created the world's creatures in three ways. One group is predominantly intellect, knowledge, and generosity; that is the angel, who knows nothing but prostration. There is no greed or passion in their element; they are absolute light, living by the love of God. Another group is void of knowledge, like animals finding beauty in fodder. They think of nothing but the stable and feed; out of wretchedness they are wise, and void of honor. This third kind is the child of Adam and human; half of him is inclined toward the higher realm, while the other half—the donkey—is inclined toward the lower. These two <note>clarification: the angels and the beasts</note> groups are at rest from war and strife, but humans are divided into three communities through trial. One group has become absolutely submerged, joined with the angels like Jesus. They are released from anger, passion, and idle talk; they have the form of a man but the meaning of Gabriel. They are freed from spiritual discipline, asceticism, and struggle. The other group has joined with the beasts; they have become pure anger and absolute desire. The house of the body was narrow and that Gabriel-like quality in them was lost. He made them dead, like a person who is soulless, for the soul that does not have the Beloved is base. Such a one lives a life lower than the animals. The deception and trickery he knows how to weave, the weaving of gold-embroidered robes, the finding of pearls in the depths of the sea, along with astronomy, medicine, and philosophy—these have no path to the seventh heaven. All of this relates to the stable <note>clarification: the material world</note>, for this science is the pillar of the beast's life. They gave these things names like "secrets of the universe," but the goal is merely the preservation of the animal for a few days.

<column-break/>

<note>original: "ایتد اوچ قسم اوزره مخلوقی بدید" (etdi üç kısm üzere mahlûku bedîd)</note>
<margin>
He made the creatures visible in three categories. Those who are angels prostrate. They became the manifestation of the love of God. Some became mixed with animality. They are heedless, wretched, and without honor. Others became prepared for both good and evil. The other half, like an angel, is noble-born. Human nature is moved by these two opposites. Man took the form of three communities. Those of the angelic rank truly reach the station of angels. They are released from anger, passion, and gossip. Do not think of them as merely human-born. The last group is of animal character, pure anger and absolute desire. The house of the body is narrow and that high quality is ruined. The soul that is without the Beloved becomes abased. This speech is the word of Truth; let it adorn your hand. He performs every precise task in the world, yet no animal can perform such deeds. He draws jewels from the depths of the sea. He is learned in philosophy, medicine, and astronomy. But he has no passage to the seventh heaven. He pays mind only to the ox and the donkey. He gave the name "mysteries" to those follies.
</margin>

It critiques worldly sciences like medicine and philosophy as being "animal sciences" if they only serve physical preservation rather than spiritual ascent.</summary>

Take a quantity of the seeds of Masha (Phaseolus radiatus).

These should be carefully separated from other articles that may have been mixed with them;

The seeds, thus separated, should be husked.

With them should be mixed a quantity of the seeds (of the same measure) of Mucuna pruriens.

They should then be thrown into meat-juice made of buffalo-flesh, that has been enriched with ghee and dressed with curds and the juice of pomegranates.

Into it should then be thrown coriander seeds, cumin seeds, and dry ginger, each of proper measure;

By eating and drinking this preparation, one obtains an abundant supply of semen. 14-15

APHRODISIAC FISH AND FLESH.

He who eats fresh fish and flesh, as also Saphari, fried in ghee, obtains an inexhaustible supply of semen. 16

CONCEPTION-INDUCING PREPARATION.

One desirous of progeny should eat 'Rohita' fish fried in ghee and boiled in such meat-juice of goat's flesh as has been dressed with the juice of fruits, and then drink the remnant (that is left in the pot) of the meat-juice itself.

TWO PREPARATIONS OF CAKE HAVING APHRODISIAC VIRTUES.

Take some fish and fowl, and cut them into pieces.

Pound these pieces with assafoedita, 'Saindhava' salt, and corriander seeds.

Add wheat flour.

Make cakes of the product, with the aid of ghee. 18

Take some fish, and cut them into pieces.

Mix with them ghee, the expressed juice of pomegranates and other fruits of the same kind, and salt.

Boil the pieces, thus mixed, in the meat-juice of buffalo flesh.

When the meat-juice enters the fish, the fish should then be pounded. (The bones should all be extracted.)

To the pounded fish should then be added pepper, cumin seeds, corriander seeds, a little assafoedita, and new ghee.

The paste that results should be used as core or kernel of cakes made of the seeds of Phaseolus radiatus. 19-20

These two preparations of cakes possess nutritive virtues. They increase one's strength. They promote cheerfulness and bring good-luck.

Capable of increasing the semen, these prove beneficial in the matter of the birth of progeny. 21

MASHA CAKES OF APHRODISIAC VIRTUES.

Take some seeds of Masha (Phaseolus radiatus), Atmagupta (Mucuna pruriens), wheat-flour, 'Sali' rice, and 'Shastika' rice, and reduce them into a paste.

A wise man having a regard for his reputation should not think of seducing a woman who is apprehensive, timid, not to be trusted, well guarded, or possessed of a father-in-law, or mother-in-law.

CHAPTER III.

EXAMINATION OF THE STATE OF A WOMAN'S MIND.

When a man is trying to gain over a woman he should examine the state of her mind, and acts as follows.

If she listens to him, but does not manifest to him in any way her own intentions, he should then try to gain her over by means of a go-between.

If she meets him once, and again comes to meet him better dressed than before, or comes to him in some lonely place, he should be certain that she is capable of being enjoyed by the use of a little force. A woman who lets a man make up to her, but does not give herself up, even after a long time, should be considered as a trifler in love, but owing to the fickleness of the human mind, even such a woman can be conquered by always keeping up a close acquaintance with her.

Burton renders freely: verse 27 is folded into the prose paragraph ending ch. II; sūtra 1 = 'When a man is trying ... acts as follows'; sūtra 2 = 'If she listens to him ... go-between'; sūtra 3 (rejects the approach yet meets him again: of two minds, win her gradually) has no clean separate rendering; 'If she meets him once ... better dressed' corresponds to sūtra 4, which the page only begins. The final sentence ('A woman who lets a man make up to her ...') is either Burton's loose rendering of sūtra 3 or the following sūtra; it is kept as the boundary.

### Chapter 3 ] Examination of Internal Sentiments. 237

A wise man should not pursue a woman who is suspicious, guarded by others, fearful, or under the constant watch of her mother-in-law, even if he feels confident in his own abilities. (27)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled Methods of Approach and Causes of Intimacy, in the fifth book concerning the wives of others <note>original: "Paradarika"</note> in the Kamasutra of the illustrious Vatsyayana.

<note>Commentary:</note> Suspicious means she has developed doubts about the suitor. Guarded means she is protected by female guards. Fearful refers to her fear of her husband. Under her mother-in-law means she is under the supervision of her mothers-in-law. One should not pursue <note>original: "na tarkayeta"</note> means one should not desire her. Knowing his own certainty <note>original: "janan-pratyayam"</note> means coming to the firm conclusion that "I am incapable of succeeding in this instance." (27)
Thus ends the forty-fourth section on Methods of Approach.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled Methods of Approach and Causes of Intimacy, in the fifth book concerning the wives of others, in the commentary on the Kamasutra of the illustrious Vatsyayana, composed by Yashodhara and titled the Jayamangala.

---

### Third Chapter.

Even when a suitor approaches them, women who are steady and bold must be tested. Because such women do not reveal their true feelings openly, the suitor cannot make a specialized approach; therefore, the examination of internal sentiments <note>original: "Bhava-pariksha"</note> is now described—
The suitor should examine the behavior of the woman; by observing her actions, her internal sentiment is examined. (1)

<note>Commentary:</note> Approaching her as one would a young maiden, he should examine her behavior, meaning her physical gestures and movements. For by examining these, her internal feelings are revealed. (1)

The author explains how such a woman is to be won—
If she does not disclose the secret matter, he should win her over through a female messenger. (2)

<note>Commentary:</note> If she does not disclose the secret <note>original: "mantram avrunanam"</note> means she does not openly reveal her desire for union. Because of her bold nature, he should win her over through a female messenger. (2)

If she rejects the initial approach but continues to associate with him, he should know that her mind is divided in two; he should win her over gradually. (3)

<note>Commentary:</note> If she rejects the approach made by the hero, but after some days have passed, she is found associating <note>original: "samsrijyamanam"</note> or moving in the hero's circles again, he should know her mind is divided. This is because she is in a state of testing herself, thinking, "I do not know what I should do." He should win her over gradually and not abandon her suddenly. (3)

The author provides a specific detail on this—
If she rejects the approach but is seen again exceptionally well-adorned, then... <note>The sentence continues on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page concludes the chapter on approaching the wives of others and begins the chapter on examining a woman's true feelings. It advises men to identify when a woman is hesitant or restricted and explains how to interpret a woman's divided mind through her social behavior.</summary>
<keywords>Kamasutra, Vatsyayana, Yashodhara, behavior examination, female messenger, courtship psychology, Jayamangala commentary</keywords>

<header> Chapter 3 ] Section on Testing the Disposition. 237 </header>

A wise man, even if he knows his own confidence, should not pursue a woman who is suspicious, guarded, fearful, or under the constant watch of her mother-in-law. 27.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled Methods of Approach and Causes of Familiarity, in the fifth book on Wives of Others in the <term>Kamasutra</term> <gloss>Aphorisms on Love</gloss> of <term>Vatsyayana</term>.

<note>Commentary:</note> Suspicious refers to one who has developed doubts about the suitor. Guarded means protected by female guards. Fearful means afraid of her husband. Under the mother-in-law means she is under the supervision of her mothers-in-law. Should not pursue means he should not desire her, even while knowing his own confidence. This means he should come to the certain conclusion that "I am powerless in this situation." 27.
This completes the forty-fourth topic: Methods of Approach.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled Methods of Approach and Causes of Familiarity, in the fifth book on Wives of Others, in the commentary of Sri <term>Vatsyayana</term>'s <term>Kamasutra</term> written by <term>Yashodhara</term> called the <term>Jayamangala</term> <gloss>The Auspicious Victory</gloss>.

---

### Chapter 3

Even when an approach is made, women who are steady and bold must be examined. Such women do not reveal their true feelings openly, and therefore a specific method of approach is not used with them. For this reason, the testing of the disposition is now discussed:

A man making an approach should examine the behavior of the woman; through that behavior, her disposition is tested. 1.

<note>Commentary:</note> Approaching her as if she were a young maiden, he should examine her behavior, meaning her physical gestures and actions. Indeed, by examining these, her internal disposition is tested. 1.

How is she to be won? He says:

If she does not reveal the secret counsel, he should win her over by means of a female messenger. 2.

<note>Commentary:</note> Does not reveal the secret counsel means she does not disclose her feelings regarding sexual union. Because of her boldness, he should win her over through a female messenger. 2.

If she rejects the approach but continues to associate with him, he should know her mind is divided in two; he should win her over gradually. 3.

<note>Commentary:</note> Rejecting the approach means she refuses the advances made by the hero. If, after some days have passed, she is found associating with him, meaning she seeks the hero's company, he should know her mind is divided in two. This is because she is in a state of testing, thinking, "I do not know what I should do." He should win her over gradually and not abandon her suddenly. 3.

Regarding this, he states a specific detail:

If she rejects the approach but is seen again specifically adorned with ornaments, then in the same way...

<summary>This page concludes the second chapter on methods of approaching women and begins the third chapter on testing their internal disposition. It advises on identifying women who are unavailable due to external constraints and how to interpret the behavior of bold women who hide their feelings.</summary>
<keywords>Kamasutra, Vatsyayana, Yashodhara, Jayamangala, testing disposition, courtship, female messenger, behavior analysis, wives of others</keywords>

# Chapter 2 ] Section on the Examination of Disposition. 237

A wise man, even if he knows his own confidence <note>clarification: in his success</note>, should not approach <note>alternative: or "presume upon"</note> a woman who is suspicious, guarded, fearful, or under the supervision of a mother-in-law. 27.

Thus ends the Second Chapter, "Approaches and Causes for Intimacy," in the Fifth Book on Adultery <note>original: "पारदारिके" (pāradārike)</note> of the Kamasutra by Sri Vatsyayana.

<margin>
Suspicious <note>clarification: means</note> having developed suspicion toward the suitor; guarded by powerful <note>clarification: guards</note>; fearful of her husband; under a mother-in-law <note>clarification: means</note> situated under the authority of mothers-in-law; he should not approach <note>clarification: means</note> he should not desire; knowing his confidence <note>clarification: means</note> attaining the certainty that "I am powerless in this case." 27.
This is the forty-fourth section, "Approaches."
Thus ends the Second Chapter, "Approaches and Causes for Intimacy," in the Fifth Book on Adultery, in the commentary on the Kamasutra of Sri Vatsyayana, written by Yashodhara and named Jayamangala.
</margin>

---

### Chapter Three.

Even when an approach is made, women who are steady, bold, and fit to be tested do not reveal their true feelings <note>original: "सद्भावा" (sadbhāvā)</note>, and therefore a specific approach toward them is not possible; thus, the "Examination of Disposition" is stated—

Making an approach, he should examine the behavior of the woman; by that, her disposition <note>term</note> <gloss>bhāva</gloss> becomes examined. 1.

<margin>
Approaching her as if she were a maiden, he should examine her behavior <note>clarification: means</note> her gestures; for by examining these, her disposition <note>term</note> <gloss>bhāva</gloss> becomes examined. 1.
</margin>

He explains how she is to be won—

If she does not disclose the secret <note>clarification: of her intention</note>, he should win her over by means of a female messenger. 2.

<margin>
"Not disclosing the secret" <note>clarification: means</note> not revealing her disposition regarding sexual union; he should win her over through a female messenger because of <note>clarification: the woman's</note> boldness. 2.
</margin>

One who rejects the approach but associates <note>clarification: with him</note> again should be known as being of two minds; he should win her over gradually. 3.

<margin>
After rejecting the approach being made by the hero, if she stays away for some days and then associates <note>clarification: means</note> enters into contact with the hero again, he should know her to be of two minds <note>clarification: torn between</note> "What should I do? I do not know," because she is testing <note>clarification: him</note>. He should win her over gradually and not abandon her suddenly. 3.
</margin>

He states a specific detail here—

One who rejects the approach but is seen again especially adorned, and in the same way—

<summary>This page concludes the chapter on approaches to women and begins the third chapter on testing a woman's disposition (bhāva). It advises on identifying women who are difficult to approach and how to interpret a woman's behavioral signals through gradual persistence and messengers.</summary>
<keywords>Vatsyayana, Kamasutra, bhāva, disposition, courtship, female messenger, Yashodhara, Jayamangala commentary</keywords>

A wise man, even if he is confident in himself, should not pursue a woman who is suspicious, guarded by others, fearful, or under the constant watch of her mother-in-law.

<margin>Suspicious means having doubts about the suitor. Guarded means watched by female guards. Fearful means afraid of her husband. Under her mother-in-law means being strictly supervised by her husband's mother. He should not pursue her, meaning he should not desire her, if he knows his own limitations. He should recognize that success there is impossible.</margin>

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Reasons for Familiarity and Making Approaches," in the fifth book on Extramarital Relations <term>Paradarika</term> <gloss>the section concerning others' wives</gloss> of Vatsyayana's Kamasutra.

<margin>This concludes the forty-fourth section on Approaches <term>Abhiyoga</term>.</margin>

Thus ends the second chapter of the fifth book on Extramarital Relations in the commentary on Vatsyayana's Kamasutra titled *Jayamangala*, composed by Yashodhara.

---

### Chapter 3: Examination of Intentions

Even when an approach is made, women who are firm or bold must be tested. Since such women do not easily reveal their true disposition, and a special approach cannot be made without knowing it, the examination of intentions <term>Bhava-pariksha</term> is now described:

While making his approach, the suitor should observe the woman's conduct; by doing so, her intentions are tested.

<margin>Just as one approaches a maiden, he should observe her conduct, meaning her gestures and movements. By observing these, her inner disposition is examined.</margin>

How is she to be won? He says:

If she does not disclose her secret thoughts, he should win her over through a female messenger.

<margin>If she does not disclose her secret thoughts, meaning she does not reveal her feelings regarding a sexual union, he should employ a female messenger because the woman is bold.</margin>

If she rejects the initial approach but continues to associate with him, he should know that her mind is divided; he should win her over gradually.

<margin>If she rejects the approach made by the hero but, after a few days have passed, she is found associating or seeking contact with him again, he should recognize that her mind is divided. Because she needs to be tested, she feels "I do not know what I should do." He should win her over gradually and not abandon her in haste.</margin>

Regarding this, he states a specific detail:

If she rejects the approach but appears again wearing more elaborate ornaments, then in the same manner...

<summary>This page concludes the second chapter of the fifth book of the Kamasutra and begins the third chapter, focusing on how a man should examine a woman's true intentions and body language before proceeding. It emphasizes the use of intermediaries and patient observation when a woman seems hesitant or conflicted.</summary>

<keywords>Vatsyayana, Kamasutra, examination of intentions, suitor, female messenger, courtship, behavior observation, Jayamangala commentary</keywords>

# Example
# Another Example

> At the arrival of the clouds <note>the rainy season</note>, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew toward Lake Manasa. One eighth of the flock flew away from the water's edge into a forest of land-growing lotuses. Oh young girl, three pairs of swans were seen playing with great passion in the water beautified by tender lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of swans in that flock. 3

**Word Order:** Oh girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of the swan flock went to Lake Manasa. One eighth part flew from the water's bank and reached the forest of land-growing lotuses. Three pairs of swans were seen enjoying play in the water adorned with young lotus shoots. Therefore, tell the entire number of the flock. 3

**Meaning:** Oh beloved girl of sixteen years! There was a group of swans. Among them, when the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root went to Lake Manasa. One eighth part of the total flew from the shore and went to a land-lotus forest. Three pairs <note>six swans</note> were seen playing with great affection in water shining with soft lotus roots. Tell me, how many swans were in that group? 3

**Statement of Problem:** <term>Mulaguna</term> <gloss>coefficient of the square root</gloss> is 10; <term>Ashtansha</term> <gloss>the eighth part</gloss> is 1/8; <term>Drishyam</term> <gloss>the visible/known quantity</gloss> is 6. Since the rule states "when increased or decreased by fractions," here we divide the known quantity and the square root coefficient by the remainder of one <note>1 minus the fraction 1/8</note>, which is 7/8. Dividing the known quantity 6 by 7/8 gives 48/7. Dividing the square root coefficient 10 by 7/8 gives 80/7. Half of this coefficient is 40/7. Its square is 1600/49. Adding this to the known quantity <note>after adjusting the denominator</note> results in 1936/49. The square root of this is 44/7. Adding half the coefficient <note>40/7</note> to this and squaring the result, the sum of the swans is found to be 144.

**Expansion:** According to the rule stated in the second verse, the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> was subtracted from one, resulting in 1 minus 1/8 equals 7/8. This was used to divide the known quantity 6, resulting in 6 divided by 7/8, which is 6 multiplied by 8/7, equaling 48/7. This became the adjusted <term>drishya rashi</term> <gloss>visible quantity</gloss>. Similarly, the square root coefficient 10 was divided by 7/8, resulting in 10 multiplied by 8/7, equaling 80/7. This became the adjusted <term>mula rashi</term> <gloss>root quantity</gloss>. Now, treating 48/7 as the known quantity and 80/7 as the square root coefficient, the calculation was performed according to the method in the previous verse. Specifically, half of the square root coefficient is 40/7. The square of this is 1600/49. This was added to the known quantity 48/7...

<meta>The page concludes mid-calculation as the sum is being added to the adjusted known quantity. The result 144 is already stated in the summary section above the expansion.</meta>

# Example
# And another example

> At the arrival of the clouds <note>the rainy season</note>, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew toward Lake Manasa. One-eighth of the flock flew away from the shore of the water to a forest of land-lotuses. O girl, three pairs of swans were seen sporting with great desire in the water beautified by young lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of the flock. 3

**Meaning:** O beloved of sixteen years of age! There was a group of swans. Among them, when the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root <note>of the total</note> went to Lake Manasaro-var. One-eighth of the flock flew from the edge of the water and went into a forest of land-lotuses. And three pairs of swans <note>totaling six</note> were seen playing very affectionately in water decorated with tender lotus stalks. So, tell me, how many swans were in that group? 3

**Numerical Setup:** The multiplier of the square root is 10; the fraction is 1/8; the visible amount <gloss>the remainder</gloss> is 6. As it was said <note>in the previous rule</note> that the values are increased or decreased by the fractions, here we divide the visible amount and the square root multiplier by the difference of the fraction from one <gloss>7/8</gloss>. The resulting visible amount is 48/7 and the square root multiplier is 80/7. Half of this multiplier is 40/7. Its square is 1600/49. Adding this <note>to the visible amount after adjustment</note> gives 1936/49. The square root of this is 44/7. Adding half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squaring the result, the quantity of swans is found to be: 144.

**Expansion:** According to the rule mentioned in the second verse, the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> was subtracted from one, resulting in 1/1 - 1/8 = 7/8. This was used to divide the visible amount of 6, resulting in 6/1 ÷ 7/8 = 6/1 × 8/7 = 48/7. After applying the conversion of seven, 48/7 became the adjusted visible quantity <term>drishya rashi</term>. Similarly, the square root multiplier of 10 was divided by 7/8, resulting in 10/1 ÷ 7/8 = 10/1 × 8/7 = 80/7. After the conversion of seven, 80/7 became the adjusted square root multiplier. Now, treating 48/7 as the visible quantity and 80/7 as the square root multiplier, the calculation was performed according to the method mentioned in the verse above. That is, half of the square root multiplier was taken, which is 40/7. This was squared to become 1600/49. This was added to the visible quantity of 48/7...

# Example
# And another example

> At the onset of the clouds <note>clarification: the rainy season</note>, ten times the square root <note>original: "मूलदशकं"</note> of a flock of swans went to Lake Manasa. One-eighth <note>original: "अष्टांशको"</note> flew from the edge of the waters to a forest of land-lilies. O young girl, three pairs of swans were seen playing with great delight in the water adorned with tender lotus-stalks. Tell me the total number of the flock <note>original: "यूथस्य संख्यां"</note>. ॥ 3 ॥

**Prose Order:** O young girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of a flock of swans went to Manasa. An eighth part flew from the shore of the waters and went to a forest of land-lilies. And three pairs of swans <note>clarification: six swans</note> were seen intent on playful sports in water shining with young lotus-stalks. Therefore, tell the total number of the flock. ॥ 3 ॥

**Meaning:** O beloved of sixteen years of age! There was a group of swans. Among them, upon the arrival of the rainy season, ten times the square root went to Lake Manasasarovar, and an eighth part flew from the water's edge and went into a forest of land-lilies, and three (3) pairs of swans were seen playing very affectionately in water beautified by tender lotus-stalks; so say, how many swans were in that group? ॥ 3 ॥

**Statement:** Square root multiplier <note>original: "मूलगुणम्"</note> 10; eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss>; visible quantity <gloss>6</gloss>. Since it was said "when increased or decreased by fractions," here, by dividing the visible and the square root multiplier by one minus the fraction <gloss>7/8</gloss>, the results are: visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>; square root multiplier <gloss>80/7</gloss>. Half the multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. The square of this <gloss>1600/49</gloss> is added <note>clarification: to the product of the multiplier and visible quantity</note> to get <gloss>1936/49</gloss>. The square root of this is <gloss>44/7</gloss>. Adding the half-multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squaring the result, the quantity of swans is produced: 144. ॥

**Expansion:** According to the rule stated in the second verse, subtracting the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> from one <note>clarification: the whole</note>, it becomes <gloss>1/1 - 1/8</gloss> = <gloss>7/8</gloss>. When the visible 6 is divided by this, <gloss>6/1 / 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>6/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>48/7</gloss>. By applying the division by seven, <gloss>48/7</gloss> became the visible quantity. Similarly, dividing the square root multiplier 10 by <gloss>7/8</gloss>, <gloss>10/1 / 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>10/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>80/7</gloss>. By dividing by seven, <gloss>80/7</gloss> became the square root multiplier. Now, taking <gloss>48/7</gloss> as the visible quantity and <gloss>80/7</gloss> as the multiplier, the operation was performed according to the method mentioned in the previous verse. That is, half of the square root multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. Squaring this <gloss>40/7</gloss>, it became <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. Adding this to the visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>...

<summary>This page presents a mathematical word problem involving a flock of swans to illustrate the solution of quadratic equations. It provides the verse, its prose meaning, and a step-by-step numerical resolution using fractional adjustments.</summary>

One-eighth of them flew from the water's edge to a forest of land-lilies. O young girl, three pairs of swans were seen playing with great joy in water adorned with tender lotus-stalks. Tell me the total number of the flock? ॥ 3 ॥

**Prose Order:** O girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of a flock of swans went to Lake <term>Manasa</term>. One-eighth part flew from the shore of the water and went to a forest of land-lilies. Three pairs of swans were seen eagerly engaged in play in water shining with young lotus-stalks. Then, tell the total number of the flock. ॥ 3 ॥

**Meaning:** O my dear sixteen-year-old beloved! There was a flock of swans. From among them, as the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root <note>original: "मूलदशकं"</note> went to Lake <term>Manasa</term>, and an eighth part flew from the edge of the water to a forest of land-lilies. As stated by the rule "when decreased or increased by parts," we divide the visible quantity and the square root multiplier by one minus the fraction <gloss>7/8</gloss>. The visible quantity becomes <gloss>48/7</gloss> and the square root multiplier becomes <gloss>80/7</gloss>. Half of the multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. Its square <gloss>1600/49</gloss> added <note>clarification: to the product of the visible quantity and 1</note> gives <gloss>1936/49</gloss>. The square root of this is <gloss>44/7</gloss>. Adding the half-multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squaring the result, the total number of swans is produced: 144.

When the visible quantity 6 is divided by this, <gloss>6/1 ÷ 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>6/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>48/7</gloss>. After performing the transformation <note>clarification: to a common denominator</note>, <gloss>48/7</gloss> becomes the visible quantity. Similarly, when the square root multiplier 10 is divided by <gloss>7/8</gloss>, <gloss>10/1 ÷ 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>10/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>80/7</gloss>. By performing the transformation, <gloss>80/7</gloss> becomes the square root multiplier. Now, taking <gloss>48/7</gloss> as the visible quantity and <gloss>80/7</gloss> as the square root multiplier, the operation is performed according to the method stated in the previous verse. That is, half of the square root multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. After squaring <gloss>40/7</gloss>, it becomes <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. Adding this to the visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>...

[context] and heaven are likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.
Ten things are roadblocks for these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.
Sloth and lack of initiative are a roadblock for wealth. Lack of adornment and decoration are a roadblock for beauty. Unsuitable activity is a roadblock for health. Bad friendship is a roadblock for ethical conduct. Lack of sense restraint is a roadblock for the spiritual life. Dishonesty is a roadblock for friends. Not rehearsing is a roadblock for learning. Not wanting to listen and ask questions are roadblocks for wisdom. Lack of commitment and reviewing are roadblocks for good qualities. Wrong practice hinders heaven.
These ten things are roadblocks for these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.
Ten things nourish these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.
Application and initiative nourish wealth. Adornment and decoration nourish beauty. Suitable activity nourishes health. Good friendship nourishes ethical conduct. Sense restraint nourishes the spiritual life. Honesty nourishes friends. Rehearsing nourishes learning. Eagerness to listen and ask questions nourishes wisdom. Commitment and reviewing nourish good qualities. Right practice nourishes heaven.
These ten things nourish these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.”

# LXXIV.

1. Dasahi bhikkhave vaḍḍhīhi vaḍḍhamāno ariyasāvako ariyāya vaḍḍhiyā vaḍḍhati, sārādāyī ca hoti varā

These, monks, are the ten things that are desired, loved, and pleasant, but difficult to obtain in the world.

3. Monks, there are ten things that act as obstacles <term>paripanthā</term> <gloss>obstructions or roadblocks</gloss> to these ten desired, loved, and pleasant things that are difficult to obtain in the world:

4. Laziness and lack of effort are an obstacle to wealth. Lack of grooming and lack of adornment are an obstacle to beauty <term>vaṇṇassa</term> <gloss>appearance or complexion</gloss>. Acting in unwholesome ways is an obstacle to health. Evil friendship is an obstacle to virtuous conduct <term>sīlānam</term>. Lack of sense restraint is an obstacle to the holy life <term>brahmacariyassa</term>. Deception is an obstacle to friendships. Lack of recitation <note>meaning the oral repetition of teachings</note> is an obstacle to great learning. Lack of desire to listen and lack of questioning are an obstacle to wisdom. Lack of application and lack of reflection are an obstacle to understanding the teachings <term>dhammānam</term>. Wrong practice is an obstacle to the heavenly realms.

These, monks, are the ten things that are obstacles to those ten desired, loved, and pleasant things that are difficult to obtain in the world.

5. Monks, there are ten things that act as nourishment <term>āhārā</term> <gloss>nutrients or supporting conditions</gloss> for these ten desired, loved, and pleasant things that are difficult to obtain in the world:

6. Diligence and effort are the nourishment for wealth. Grooming and adornment are the nourishment for beauty. Acting in wholesome ways is the nourishment for health. Good friendship is the nourishment for virtuous conduct. Sense restraint is the nourishment for the holy life. Honesty is the nourishment for friendships. Recitation is the nourishment for great learning. The desire to listen and the habit of questioning are the nourishment for wisdom. Application and reflection are the nourishment for understanding the teachings. Right practice is the nourishment for the heavenly realms.

These, monks, are the ten things that are the nourishment for those ten desired, loved, and pleasant things that are difficult to obtain in the world.

4. Laziness and lack of effort are an obstacle to wealth. Lack of grooming and lack of adornment are an obstacle to beauty <note>original: "vaṇṇassa", referring to physical appearance or complexion</note>. Engaging in unsuitable activities is an obstacle to health. Evil friendship is an obstacle to virtuous conduct. Lack of sense restraint is an obstacle to the holy life <note>original: "brahmacariyassa"</note>. Deception is an obstacle to friendships. Lack of recitation is an obstacle to great learning. Lack of desire to listen and lack of questioning are an obstacle to wisdom. Lack of application and lack of reflection are an obstacle to the teachings <note>original: "dhammānam"</note>. Wrong practice is an obstacle to the heavenly realms.

Regarding these ten things, monks, which are desired, pleasant, and agreeable, but difficult to obtain in the world, these are the ten obstacles.

5. Regarding these ten things, monks, which are desired, pleasant, and agreeable, but difficult to obtain in the world, there are ten nourishments <note>original: "āhārā", used here metaphorically as things that sustain or bring about a result</note>:

6. Diligence and effort are the nourishment for wealth. Grooming and adornment are the nourishment for beauty. Engaging in suitable activities is the nourishment for health. Good friendship is the nourishment for virtuous conduct. Sense restraint is the nourishment for the holy life. Honesty is the nourishment for friendships. Recitation is the nourishment for great learning. The desire to listen and questioning are the nourishment for wisdom. Application and reflection are the nourishment for the teachings. Right practice is the nourishment for the heavenly realms.

Regarding these ten things, monks, which are desired, pleasant, and agreeable, but difficult to obtain in the world, these are the ten nourishments.

5. Regarding these ten things, monks, which are desired, loved, and agreeable, but difficult to obtain in the world, there are ten things that are nutriment <note>original: "āhārā"</note> <note>clarification: or supports</note>:

<header>MAHÂ-VAGGA. [III. 61. 2.</header>

Tyâham evam vadâmi :—Tena h' âyasmanto pânâtipâtino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, adinnâdâyino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, abrahmacârino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, musâvâdino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, pisuṇâvâcâ¹ bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, pharusâvâcâ¹ bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, samphappalâpino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, abhijhâluno bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, vyâpannacittâ bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, micchâdiṭṭhikâ bhavissanti pubbe katahetu. Pubbe katam kho pana bhikkhave sârato paccâgacchatam² na hoti chando vâ vâyâmo vâ idam vâ karaṇîyam idam vâ akaraṇîyan ti. Iti karaṇîyâkaraṇîye kho pana saccato thetato aupapabhbiyamâne muṭṭhasatinam anârakkhânam viharatam na hoti paccattam sahadhammiko samaṇavâdo.

Ayam kho me bhikkhave tesu samaṇabrâhmaṇesu evamvâdisu evamdiṭṭhisu paṭhamo sahadhammiko niggaho hoti.

3. Tatra bhikkhave ye te samaṇabrâhmaṇâ evamvâdino evamdiṭṭhino—yam kiñcâyam purisapuggalo paṭisamvedeti sukham vâ dukkham vâ adukkhamasukham vâ sabbam tam issaranimmânahetu ti tyâham upasaṅkamitvâ evam vadâmi :—Saccam kira tumhe âyasmanto evamvâdino evamdiṭṭhino—yam kiñcâyam purisapuggalo paṭisamvedeti sukham vâ dukkham vâ adukkhamasukham vâ sabbam tam issaranimmânahetu ti?

Te ce me evam puṭṭhâ âmâ³ ti paṭijânanti.

Tyâham evam vadâmi :—Tena h' âyasmanto pânâtipâtino bhavissanti issaranimmânahetu . . . pe . . . micchâdiṭṭhino bhavissanti issaranimmânahetu. Issaranimmânânam kho pana bhikkhave sârato paccâgacchatam na hoti chando vâ vâyâmo vâ idam vâ karaṇîyam idam vâ akaraṇîyan ti. Iti karaṇîyâkaraṇîye kho pana saccato thetato anupalabbhiyamâne muṭṭhasatinam anârakkhânam viharatam na hoti paccattam sahadhammiko samaṇavâdo.

Ayam kho me bhikkhave tesu samaṇabrâhmaṇesu evamvâdisu evamdiṭṭhisu dutiyo sahadhammiko niggaho hoti.

---

[context] There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:
[context] ‘Everything this individual person experiences—pleasurable, painful, or neutral—has no cause or reason.’
[context] Regarding this, I went up to the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that
everything an individual person experiences is because of past deeds, and I said to them:
‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’
And they answered, ‘Yes’.
I said to them:
‘In that case, you might kill living creatures, steal, be unchaste; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; be covetous, malicious, or have wrong view, all because of past deeds.’
Those who believe that past deeds are the most important thing have no enthusiasm or effort, no idea that there are things that should and should not be done.
Not finding as a genuine fact that there are things that should and should not be done, they’re unmindful and careless, and can’t rightly be called ascetics.
This is my first legitimate refutation of the ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view.
Regarding this, I went up to the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that
everything that an individual person experiences is because of God Almighty’s creation, and I said to them:
‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’
And they answered, ‘Yes’.
I said to them:
‘In that case, you might kill living creatures, steal, be unchaste; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; be covetous, malicious, or have wrong view, all because of God Almighty’s creation.’
Those who believe that God Almighty’s creative power is the most important thing have no enthusiasm, no effort, no idea that there are things that should and should not be done.
Not finding as a genuine fact that there are things that should and should not be done, they’re unmindful and careless, and can’t rightly be called ascetics.
This is my second legitimate refutation of the ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view.
Regarding this, I went up to the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that
everything that an individual person experiences has no cause or reason, and I said to them:

And they answered, ‘Yes’.
I said to them:
‘In that case, you might kill living creatures, steal, be unchaste; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; be covetous, malicious, or have wrong view, all without cause or reason.’
Those who believe that the absence of cause or reason is the most important thing have no enthusiasm, no effort, no idea that there are things that should and should not be done.
Not finding as a genuine fact that there are things that should and should not be done, they’re unmindful and careless, and can’t rightly be called ascetics.
[context] This is my third legitimate refutation of the ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view.
[context] These are the three sectarian tenets—as pursued, pressed, and grilled by the astute—which, when taken to their conclusion, end with inaction.
[context] But the Dhamma that I’ve taught is irrefutable, uncorrupted, beyond reproach, and not scorned by sensible ascetics and brahmins.
