# The Great Section <note>original: Mahâ-vagga</note>

To them, I say this: "Then, venerable sirs, you would be killers of living beings <term>pânâtipâtino</term> because of past actions. You would be takers of what is not given <term>adinnâdâyino</term> because of past actions. You would be unchaste <term>abrahmacârino</term> because of past actions. You would be speakers of lies <term>musâvâdino</term> because of past actions. You would be speakers of slander <term>pisuṇâvâcâ</term> because of past actions. You would be speakers of harsh words <term>pharusâvâcâ</term> because of past actions. You would be speakers of idle chatter <term>samphappalâpino</term> because of past actions. You would be covetous <term>abhijhâluno</term> because of past actions. You would be ill-willed <term>vyâpannacittâ</term> because of past actions. You would be holders of wrong view <term>micchâdiṭṭhikâ</term> because of past actions."

Monks, for those who fall back on past actions as the essential truth <note>referring to the belief that every current experience is strictly determined by previous lives</note>, there is no desire to act, no effort, and no sense of "this should be done" or "this should not be done." Since what should and should not be done is not found to be true or established, those who live with muddled mindfulness and lack of restraint cannot legitimately claim to be true ascetics.

This, monks, is my first justified rebuke <term>sahadhammiko niggaho</term> of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such doctrines and views.

3. In this case, monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this doctrine and view: "Whatever pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling a person experiences is all caused by the creation of a supreme deity <term>issaranimmânahetu</term>." I approach them and say: "Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold this doctrine and view: that whatever a person experiences—pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling—is all caused by the creation of a supreme deity?"

When they are asked this by me, they admit it, saying, "Yes."

Then I say to them: "Then, venerable sirs, you would be killers of living beings because of the creation of a supreme deity... <note>the text here uses the abbreviation "pe" to indicate the repetition of the previous list of ten unwholesome actions</note> ...you would be holders of wrong view because of the creation of a supreme deity." Monks, for those who fall back on the creation of a supreme deity as the essential truth, there is no desire to act, no effort, and no sense of "this should be done" or "this should not be done." Since what should and should not be done is not found to be true or established, those who live with muddled mindfulness and lack of restraint cannot legitimately claim to be true ascetics.

This, monks, is my second justified rebuke of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such doctrines and views.

<margin>1. All manuscripts read <term>pisuṇâvâcâ</term> and <term>pharusâvâcâ</term>.</margin>
<margin>2. The manuscripts here and below vary between <term>gacchantam</term> and <term>gacchatam</term>.</margin>
<margin>3. Manuscripts D. and T. read <term>âmo</term>.</margin>

<summary>The Buddha critiques deterministic views of causality, arguing that attributing all current experiences to past lives or divine creation removes individual moral responsibility and the motivation for spiritual practice. He lists ten unwholesome actions that would be unavoidable under such fatalistic frameworks.</summary>
<keywords>causality, fatalism, divine creation, ethics, moral responsibility, unwholesome actions, asceticism</keywords>

### The Great Section <note>original: Mahâ-vagga</note>

I say this to them: "Then, venerable sirs, you will be those who take life <term>pânâtipâtino</term> because of what was done in the past. You will be those who take what is not given <term>adinnâdâyino</term> because of what was done in the past. You will be those who are unchaste <term>abrahmacârino</term> because of what was done in the past. You will be those who speak lies <term>musâvâdino</term> because of what was done in the past. You will be those who speak slander <term>pisuṇâvâcâ</term> because of what was done in the past. You will be those who speak harshly <term>pharusâvâcâ</term> because of what was done in the past. You will be those who indulge in idle chatter <term>samphappalâpino</term> because of what was done in the past. You will be those who are covetous <term>abhijhâluno</term> because of what was done in the past. You will be those who have a mind of ill-will <term>vyâpannacittâ</term> because of what was done in the past. You will be those who hold wrong views <term>micchâdiṭṭhikâ</term> because of what was done in the past."

Monks, for those who fall back on the idea that past deeds are the essential truth, there is no desire to act, no effort, and no sense that "this should be done" or "this should not be done." Since one does not truly and firmly find a basis for what should or should not be done, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without self-protection lack any justified, righteous claim to being a true ascetic.

Monks, this is my first righteous refutation <term>sahadhammiko niggaho</term> of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such doctrines and views.

3. In this regard, monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this doctrine and view: "Whatever pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling a person experiences, all of it is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord <term>issaranimmânahetu</term>." I go to them and say: "Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold the doctrine and view that whatever pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling a person experiences is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord?"

When I ask them this, if they acknowledge it and say "Yes,"

I say to them: "Then, venerable sirs, you will be those who take life because of the creation of a Supreme Lord... <note>The text indicates the previous list of ten unwholesome actions repeats here</note> ...you will be those who hold wrong views because of the creation of a Supreme Lord." Monks, for those who fall back on the idea that the creation of a Supreme Lord is the essential truth, there is no desire to act, no effort, and no sense that "this should be done" or "this should not be done." Since one does not truly and firmly find a basis for what should or should not be done, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without self-protection lack any justified, righteous claim to being a true ascetic.

Monks, this is my second righteous refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such doctrines and views.

---
<margin>1. All manuscripts read pisuṇâvâcâ and pharusâvâcâ. Compare below XVI. 8.</margin>
<margin>2. The manuscripts here and below vary between gacchantam and gacchatam.</margin>
<margin>3. Manuscripts D. and T. read âmo.</margin>

<summary>The Buddha refutes the doctrines of fatalism and theism by arguing that if all actions were predetermined by past deeds or a creator god, human effort and moral responsibility would be meaningless. This represents the first two of three "righteous refutations" against flawed philosophical views regarding the causes of human experience.</summary>
<keywords>determinism, fatalism, theism, moral responsibility, refutation, asceticism, karma, Supreme Lord</keywords>

# THE GREAT SECTION <note>original: "MAHÂ-VAGGA"</note>

To them I say this: "Then, venerable sirs, you will be takers of life <note>original: "pânâtipâtino"</note> because of what was done in the past, you will be takers of what is not given <note>original: "adinnâdâyino"</note> because of what was done in the past, you will be unchaste <note>original: "abrahmacârino"</note> because of what was done in the past, you will be speakers of lies <note>original: "musâvâdino"</note> because of what was done in the past, you will be speakers of slanderous speech <note>original: "pisuṇâvâcâ"</note> <margin>All manuscripts <note>clarification: read</note> pisuṇâvâcâ and pharusâvâcâ (Compare below XVI. 8).</margin> because of what was done in the past, you will be speakers of harsh speech <note>original: "pharusâvâcâ"</note> because of what was done in the past, you will be speakers of frivolous chatter <note>original: "samphappalâpino"</note> because of what was done in the past, you will be covetous <note>original: "abhijhâluno"</note> because of what was done in the past, you will be malicious-minded <note>original: "vyâpannacittâ"</note> because of what was done in the past, you will be ones of wrong view <note>original: "micchâdiṭṭhikâ"</note> because of what was done in the past." For those, monks, who fall back upon <note>original: "paccâgacchatam"</note> <margin>The manuscripts here and below vary between gacchantam and gacchatam.</margin> what was done in the past as the essence, there is no desire <note>original: "chando"</note> or effort <note>original: "vâyâmo"</note> <note>clarification: regarding</note> "this is to be done" or "this is not to be done." Thus, when what is to be done and what is not to be done are not truly and reliably found, for those living with muddled mindfulness and without protection, there is no personal, legitimate ascetic-statement <note>original: "sahadhammiko samaṇavâdo"</note>.

This, monks, is my first legitimate refutation <note>original: "sahadhammiko niggaho"</note> of those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such views.

3. Therein, monks, regarding those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such views—"Whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is due to the creation of a Supreme Lord" <note>original: "issaranimmânahetu"</note>—I go to them and say this: "Is it true, venerable sirs, that you speak thus and hold such views—that whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is due to the creation of a Supreme Lord?"

If, when asked by me, they acknowledge it, saying "Yes" <note>original: "âmâ"</note>, <margin>D., T. <note>clarification: manuscripts read</note> âmo.</margin>

To them I say this: "Then, venerable sirs, you will be takers of life because of the creation of a Supreme Lord . . . <term>pe</term> <gloss>abbreviation for 'and so on'</gloss> . . . you will be ones of wrong view because of the creation of a Supreme Lord. For those, monks, who fall back upon the creation of a Supreme Lord as the essence, there is no desire or effort <note>clarification: regarding</note> 'this is to be done' or 'this is not to be done.' Thus, when what is to be done and what is not to be done are not truly and reliably found, for those living with muddled mindfulness and without protection, there is no personal, legitimate ascetic-statement."

This, monks, is my second legitimate refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such views.

<summary>The Buddha refutes the views of fatalism based on past actions and theism based on a creator's will, arguing that both eliminate personal agency and moral responsibility.</summary>
<keywords>determinism, theism, moral responsibility, refutation, ethics, karma, creator god</keywords>

To them, I say this: "In that case, venerable sirs, people will be killers of living beings <note>original: "pânâtipâtino"</note> because of what was done in the past. They will be takers of what is not given <note>original: "adinnâdâyino"</note> because of what was done in the past. They will be unchaste <note>original: "abrahmacârino"</note> because of what was done in the past. They will be liars <note>original: "musâvâdino"</note> because of what was done in the past. They will be slanderers <note>original: "pisuṇâvâcâ"</note> because of what was done in the past. They will be harsh of speech <note>original: "pharusâvâcâ"</note> because of what was done in the past. They will be frivolous talkers <note>original: "samphappalâpino"</note> because of what was done in the past. They will be covetous <note>original: "abhijhâluno"</note> because of what was done in the past. They will be ill-willed <note>original: "vyâpannacittâ"</note> because of what was done in the past. They will be of wrong view <note>original: "micchâdiṭṭhikâ"</note> because of what was done in the past." Monks, for those who fall back on what was done in the past as the essential truth, there is no desire or effort regarding what should be done or what should not be done. Thus, when what should and should not be done is not truly and firmly established, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without self-protection have no legitimate personal claim to being contemplatives.

<margin>1. All manuscripts read "pisuṇâvâcâ" and "pharusâvâcâ" (compare below XVI. 8).</margin>
<margin>2. The manuscripts here and below vary between "gacchantam" and "gatatam".</margin>

This, monks, is my first legitimate refutation <note>original: "sahadhammiko niggaho"</note> of those recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view.

3. There, monks, are those recluses and brahmins who hold this doctrine and view: "Whatever a person experiences, whether pleasant, painful, or neutral, all of it is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord <note>original: "issaranimmânahetu"</note>." I go to them and say: "Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold such a doctrine and view?"

When I ask them this, if they acknowledge it, saying, "Yes" <note>original: "âmâ"</note>,

<margin>3. Manuscripts D and T read "âmo".</margin>

I say to them: "In that case, venerable sirs, people will be killers of living beings because of the creation of a Supreme Lord... and so on... they will be of wrong view because of the creation of a Supreme Lord. Monks, for those who fall back on the creation of a Supreme Lord as the essential truth, there is no desire or effort regarding what should be done or what should not be done. Thus, when what should and should not be done is not truly and firmly established, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without self-protection have no legitimate personal claim to being contemplatives."

This, monks, is my second legitimate refutation of those recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view.

<summary>The Buddha refutes deterministic views that attribute all human experience solely to past actions or the will of a Supreme Lord, arguing such views eliminate moral responsibility and the need for effort.</summary>
<keywords>determinism, fatalism, karma, Supreme Lord, moral responsibility, refutation, ethics</keywords>

Therefore he does not censure men, and men do not censure him. The perfect man does not seek to be heard of; how is it that you delight in doing so?'

Confucius said, 'Excellent;' and thereupon he took leave of his associates, forsook his disciples, retired to the neighbourhood of a great marsh, wore skins and hair cloth, and ate acorns and chestnuts. He went among animals without causing any confusion among their herds, and among birds without troubling their movements. Birds and beasts did not dislike him; how much less would men do so!

5. Confucius asked Ȝze-sang Hû, saying, 'I was twice driven from Lû; the tree was felled over me in Sung; I was obliged to disappear from Wei; I was reduced to extreme distress in Shang and Kâu; and I was kept in a state of siege between Khăn and Ȝhâi. I have encountered these various calamities; my intimate associates are removed from me more and more; my followers and friends are more and more dispersed;—why have all these things befallen me?'

<meta>The text contains Chapter 48 and the beginning of Chapter 49 of the Tao Te Ching, featuring commentaries by Su Zhe, Lü Huiqing, Huang Maocai, and Xizhai.</meta>

<margin><term>Su</term> <gloss>Su Zhe, 1039–1112 AD</gloss>’s Commentary</margin> Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but devote themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily. However, without a single principle to unify this knowledge, they cannot avoid it becoming a burden. Confucius said: To hear much and select what is good to follow, or to see much and remember it, is only the second level of knowledge. If one day you know the Way, you will look back on worldly deceptions and see that nothing is not a delusion. Removing delusion and returning to one's true nature is what is called "decreasing." Confucius asked Zigong: Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all? Zigong replied: Yes, is it not so? Confucius said: No, I have one thread that runs through it all. To forget the mind in order to restore nature to purity is called decreasing. When delusions no longer remain and one reaches the point where even this forgetting is forgotten, nature is restored to purity without any remainder. Then one removes "doing" and does not fail to reach <term>Wu Wei</term> <gloss>non-action or effortless action</gloss>. Everyone has the desire to take hold of the world and manage its affairs, so they create activities and seek results. When this seeking mind is visible externally, things and people resist it, making success difficult. The Sage practices non-action and thus has no ulterior business in his mind. When this is visible externally, all things are at peace with him. Though he does not strive to take the world or manage its affairs, the affairs of the world follow him and are settled peacefully.

<margin><term>Lü</term> <gloss>Lü Huiqing, 1032–1111 AD</gloss>’s Commentary</margin> Practicing learning is for those who have not yet heard the Way. Because they have not heard it, their search must be broad, thus it is called "daily increase." Practicing the Way is for those who have already heard the Way. Having heard it, their practice must be nothing other than non-action, thus it is called "daily decrease." To "decrease and further decrease" refers to those who have not yet escaped the realm of "doing." One must even decrease the act of decreasing itself. Only then does one reach non-action. Non-action means being still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" means responding and thus penetrating the causes of all things under heaven. Reaching non-action through the process of non-action is called the constant path. Learning without worry is called divine. The direction of the divine is what is called the Way. Who can attain such supreme divinity? From this we can see that winning the world is always done through non-action. If one resorts to "doing," it is clear that such a person is not fit to win the world.

<column-break/>

<margin><term>Huang Maocai</term> <gloss>A Song Dynasty scholar</gloss>’s Commentary</margin> Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning, therefore learning desires daily increase. Only after reaching the state where nothing is forced can one speak of the Way, therefore the Way desires daily decrease. However, increase can be sought through progress, while decrease is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only those of supreme clarity can suddenly cast off attachments and reach the realm of non-action. Thus they can leave nothing undone, and their practical application is inexhaustible. When applied to the world, they have more than enough room to maneuver.

<margin><term>Xizhai</term> <gloss>The scholar Li Zhicai</gloss>’s Commentary</margin> The purpose of learning is to seek knowledge, so it increases daily. The purpose of the Way is to remove delusion, so it decreases daily. If knowledge is not perfected, the decrease will not be complete. Therefore, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then one reaches non-action. Upon reaching non-action, even when there is action, it has never ceased to be "non-action." This cannot easily be discussed in terms of mere increase or decrease. When non-action reaches its peak, despite the vastness of the world, a single thread runs through it. If one uses meddlesome activity to create more business, even a single object beforehand will become entangled and confused; how much more so the vastness of the world?

The Sage has no constant heart <note>or "fixed mind"</note>; he takes the heart of the people as his own. To those who are good, I am good. To those who are not good, I am also good. Thus, Virtue is goodness. To those who are trustful, I am trustful. To those who are not trustful, I am also trustful. Thus, Virtue is trust. The Sage dwells in the world with a cautious and merging mind; for the sake of the world, he makes his heart murky <note>meaning undifferentiated or simple</note>. The people all fix their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage <unclear>treats them all as his children.</unclear>

<page-num>Twenty-two</page-num>

<meta>This page contains commentary on Chapters 48 and 49 of the Tao Te Ching, focusing on the concepts of "daily gain" versus "daily loss" and the Sage's lack of a fixed mind.</meta>

<margin>Su's Commentary <note>Su Zhe, 1039–1112, a prominent Song dynasty scholar</note></margin>Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but devote themselves to learning find that what they hear and see increases daily. Yet, having no means to unify this knowledge, it inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day you know the Way, you will look back on all artificiality and false actions as nothing but delusions. To remove delusion and return to one's true nature is what is called "loss." Confucius asked Zigong: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with one principle." Forgetting the calculating mind to purely return to nature is called loss. When delusion no longer exists, and one eventually forgets even this seeking mind to return fully to nature, then there is nothing left. Then one removes "doing" and does not fail to reach <term>Wu Wei</term> <gloss>Non-action or effortless action</gloss>. All people have the desire to take hold of the world and finish its affairs; thus they manufacture tasks and seek results. This intent is visible externally, and things resist it; therefore, difficulty arises and success is not achieved. The Sage practices Non-action and thus his mind is free of affairs. This is visible externally and things are at peace with him. Although he does not strive to take the world or manage its affairs, the affairs of the world follow him and find peace.

<margin>Lü's Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032–1111, a scholar known for blending Taoism and Buddhism</note></margin>Devoting oneself to learning is for those who have not yet heard the Way. Those who seek it without hearing it must be broad in their pursuit; hence it is called "daily gain." Devoting oneself to the Way is for those who have already heard it. Having heard it, one must act by simply doing nothing; hence it is called "daily loss." To "lose and lose again" means that one has not yet escaped "doing." One must even lose the act of losing itself. Only then does one reach Non-action. Non-action refers to being silent and unmoving. "Nothing is left undone" refers to being moved and subsequently penetrating all the causes under heaven. Reaching Non-action through Non-action is what is called the constant. Learning without worry is called "divine." The direction of the divine is the Way. Who but the most divine can participate in this? From this perspective, one always takes the world through Non-action. When it comes to "doing," it is clear that such is insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai's Commentary <note>A Southern Song dynasty scholar</note></margin>Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning; thus, learning desires daily gain. Only after there is nothing one "does" can one speak of the Way; thus, the Way desires daily loss. However, gain can be sought through progress, while loss is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly let go and drop everything, reaching the realm of Non-action. Thus they can leave nothing undone, and their practical application is inexhaustible. When applied to the world, they have more than enough room to maneuver.

<margin>Xizhai's Commentary <note>Referring to Li Daochun, a 13th-century Taoist master</note></margin>Devoting oneself to learning is the means to seek knowledge; therefore, there is daily gain. Devoting oneself to the Way is the means to remove delusion; therefore, there is daily loss. If knowledge is not ultimate, then the loss is not complete; thus, daily gain is the foundation for daily loss. If one loses and loses again until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then there is Non-action. Upon reaching Non-action, then even "having action" is never anything but "non-action." This cannot be easily discussed in terms of gain and loss. When Non-action reaches its ultimate state, though the things of the world are many, one unifies them. If one creates trouble by being meddlesome, even a single thing in front of one remains entangled and chaotic, let alone the many things of the world.

The Sage has no constant mind; he takes the mind of the people as his own mind. Those who are good, I treat as good. Those who are not good, I also treat as good; thus, virtue is goodness. Those who are faithful, I trust. Those who are not faithful, I also trust; thus, virtue is trust. The Sage is in the world, shrinking back for the sake of the world, making his heart turbid <note>meaning undifferentiated or simple</note>. The people all fix their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage <note>text continues on next page</note>

<page-num>22</page-num>
<sig>The Primal Wings of Laozi, Volume Two</sig>

<summary>This page features commentaries on the Tao Te Ching's philosophy of "daily loss" to reach Non-action and the Sage's empathetic, non-judgmental approach to the people. Various scholars explain that while intellectual learning requires accumulation, spiritual mastery requires the shedding of artificiality and ego.</summary>
<keywords>Tao, Wu Wei, Non-action, learning, daily loss, Su Zhe, Lü Huiqing, virtue, Sage, people's mind</keywords>

<meta>This page contains commentary on Chapters 48 and 49 of the Tao Te Ching, featuring notes from Su Che, Lü Huiqing, Huang Maocai, and Li Zhichang (Xizhai).</meta>

<margin>Su's Commentary <note>context: Su Che (1039–1112), a prominent Song dynasty official and scholar.</note></margin>Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>Way</gloss> and yet devote themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily; yet, having no way to unify it <note>clarification: these observations</note>, they cannot avoid being burdened by it. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day one knows the <term>Tao</term>, one looks back at the false and the artificial; there is nothing that is not delusional. To remove the delusion and return to <term>xing</term> <gloss>nature/essence</gloss> is what is called "decreasing." Confucius said to Zigong: "Do you think of me as one who studies much and remembers it all?" He replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with one <note>clarification: principle</note>." Forgetting the mind to purely return to nature is called decreasing; yet if delusions still remain, one must continue until one also forgets this <note>clarification: very act of</note> forgetting. When the mind is pure and one returns to nature without residue, then one removes <term>wei</term> <gloss>purposeful action</gloss> and does not fail to reach <term>wu wei</term> <gloss>non-action</gloss>. All people have desires and the heart <note>clarification: or mind</note> to take hold of the world's affairs; thus they create business and seek things. Their heart is manifested outwardly and things <note>clarification: the world</note> loathe them, therefore they find difficulty and do not succeed. The Sage practices non-action and therefore has no business <note>clarification: or ulterior motives</note> in his heart. It is manifested outwardly and things are at peace with it. Though he does not <note>clarification: actively</note> take the world's affairs to act upon them, the affairs of the world follow him and are at peace.

<margin>Lü's Commentary <note>context: Lü Huiqing (1032–1111), a high-ranking official and reformer of the Song dynasty.</note></margin>To practice learning is for those who have not yet heard the <term>Tao</term>. Those who have not heard the <term>Tao</term> and seek it cannot help but be broad; therefore it is said: "it increases." To practice the <term>Tao</term> is for those who have already heard the <term>Tao</term>. Those who have already heard the <term>Tao</term> and practice it cannot help but practice non-action; therefore it is said: "it decreases." To decrease and further decrease means one has not yet avoided having <note>clarification: some</note> action. One must even decrease that which does the decreasing, and only then reach non-action. Non-action refers to being still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" <note>original: "無不為"</note> refers to being stimulated and then penetrating the causes of all under heaven. To reach non-action through decreasing: this is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called <term>shen</term> <gloss>spirit/divine</gloss>. The direction of the spirit is what is called the <term>Tao</term>. As for the ultimate spirit, who can equal this? From this we see that taking the world is always done through non-action. As for those who use <term>you wei</term> <gloss>purposeful action</gloss>, we can know they are insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai's Commentary <note>context: A Southern Song dynasty scholar and official.</note></margin>Only after there is nothing one does not know can one speak of learning; thus learning desires daily increase. Only after there is nothing one does not do can one speak of the <term>Tao</term>; thus the <term>Tao</term> desires daily decrease. However, that which increases can be sought through progress, while that which decreases is sometimes difficult to attain through force. Only those of ultimate clarity can suddenly drop <note>clarification: their burdens</note> and reach the realm of non-action. Thus they are able to leave nothing undone, and their applications are inexhaustible, acting upon the world with great ease.

<margin>Xizhai's Commentary <note>context: Li Zhichang (1193–1256), a Quanzhen Daoist leader.</note></margin>Practicing learning is the means by which one seeks knowledge, thus it increases daily. Practicing the <term>Tao</term> is the means by which one removes delusion, thus it decreases daily. If knowledge is not ultimate, then the decrease is not complete; therefore, daily increase is the ground for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is complete, then there is non-action. As for reaching non-action, then in every instance of having action, there is nothing that is not non-action. This is not easily discussed in terms of decrease and increase. When non-action reaches its limit, though the world is vast, one unifies it with one <note>clarification: principle</note>. If one uses "having business" <note>original: "有事"</note> to create business, it is difficult to find leisure; even a single object before one remains entangled and confused, so how much more so for the vastness of the world?

The Sage has no constant heart <note>clarification: or fixed mind</note>; he takes the heart of the people as his heart. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good; thus virtue <note>alternative: or "the power of the Way"</note> is goodness. To those who are faithful, I am faithful; to those who are not faithful, I am also faithful; thus virtue is faithfulness. The Sage is in the world, shrinking back <note>original: "惛惛"</note>, making his heart turbid for the sake of the world. The people all focus their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage <note>clarification: treats them all as children</note>.

<summary>This page contains various scholarly commentaries on the Daoist principles of "daily increase" in learning versus "daily decrease" in the Tao, concluding with the start of Chapter 49 regarding the Sage's impartial heart toward the people.</summary>
<keywords>Tao, Wu Wei, non-action, learning, virtue, Sage, Su Che, Lü Huiqing, Xizhai, daily decrease</keywords>

<meta>This page contains commentaries on Chapter 48 and the beginning of Chapter 49 of the Tao Te Ching. The commentaries are attributed to Su Che, Lu Huiqing, Huang Maocai, and Xi Zhai.</meta>

<margin>Commentary by Su <note>context: Su Che (1039–1112), a prominent Song dynasty statesman and scholar.</note></margin> One who does not know the Way <term>Tao</term> and yet devotes himself to learning will find that what he hears and sees increases daily. If he has no means to unify this knowledge, it inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day a person comes to know the Way, they will look back on their former pretenses and artificial actions as entirely false. By removing the false and returning to one's true nature, this is called "decreasing." Confucius said to Zigong: "Do you think I am one who learns many things and remembers them?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I pervade them all with a single thread." When the mind is forgotten in order to return purely to nature, this is called "decreasing." Yet as long as any trace of falseness remains, one must continue until even this forgetting is forgotten, and the nature is restored without residue. Then one moves beyond action <term>wei</term> and does not fail to reach non-action <term>wu wei</term>. All people have desires and a mind that seeks to take hold of the world and its affairs. Therefore, when they initiate actions and seek results, their intentions are visible externally, and things resist them; thus, they meet difficulties and fail. The Sage practices non-action and therefore has no "affairs" in his mind. This is visible externally, and things are at peace with him. Though he does not seek to take the world or manage its affairs, the world and its affairs naturally settle into order through him.

<margin>Commentary by Lu <note>context: Lu Huiqing (1035–1111), a high-ranking official and reformer of the Northern Song dynasty.</note></margin> Engaging in learning <term>wei xue</term> is for those who have not yet heard the Way. When one seeks what has not been heard, one cannot help but be broad; thus it is said to "increase daily." Engaging in the Way <term>wei tao</term> is for those who have already heard the Way. Once it is heard, one cannot help but practice non-action; thus it is said to "decrease daily." To "decrease and further decrease" implies that one has not yet escaped the realm of purposeful action. Only by decreasing the "decreaser" itself does one reach non-action. Non-action means to be still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" means that when stimulated, one penetrates all the causes under heaven. Reaching non-action through the process of non-action is what is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called spirit. The direction of the spirit is what is called the Way. Who but the most spiritual can attain this? From this we see that taking the world is always done through non-action. As for using purposeful action, it is clear that such is insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin> Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning seeks daily increase. Only after reaching a state where nothing is done for a purpose can one speak of the Way; therefore, the Way seeks daily decrease. That which increases can be sought through progress, but that which decreases is sometimes difficult to achieve through forceful effort. Only the most enlightened can suddenly cast everything off and reach the realm of non-action. Thus, they can do everything, and their practical application is inexhaustible, acting upon the world with effortless ease.

<margin>Commentary by Xi Zhai</margin> Engaging in learning is the means to seek knowledge, thus it increases daily. Engaging in the Way is the means to remove the false, thus it decreases daily. If knowledge is not perfected, the decreasing will not be complete; therefore, daily increase provides the ground for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until the false is gone and the true is whole, then one reaches non-action. Once non-action is reached, then every purposeful action is essentially non-action; this is something that cannot easily be discussed in terms of mere "increase" or "decrease." When non-action reaches its peak, though the things of the world are many, they are unified by a single thread. If one attempts to handle the world through purposeful interference, even a single object creates entanglement and error; how much worse would it be with the vastness of the world?

The Sage has no fixed mind; he takes the mind of the people as his own. To those who are good, I am good. To those who are not good, I am also good; thus virtue is goodness. To those who are trustful, I trust them. To those who are not trustful, I also trust them; thus virtue is trust. The Sage dwells in the world with a blurred and settled mind, making the mind of the world muddy and undifferentiated. The people all focus their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage <unclear>treats them all as children</unclear>.

<summary>This page contains scholar commentaries on the paradox of "daily increase" in learning versus "daily decrease" in the Way, concluding with the start of Chapter 49 on the Sage's impartial mind.</summary>
<keywords>Tao, Wu Wei, Non-action, Sage, Learning, Virtue, Trust, Su Che, Lu Huiqing</keywords>

倒用板子棍子，就站著，不知他拿什麼東西，打了一頓，臉上打破了兩處。我們聽見姨太太這裡有一種藥，上棒瘡的，姑娘尋一丸給我呢。」

寶釵聽了，忙命鶯兒去找了兩丸來與平兒。寶釵道：「既這樣，你去替我問候罷，我就不去了。」平兒向寶釵答應著去了。不在話下。

且說香菱見了眾人之後，吃過晚飯，寶釵等都往買母處去，自己便往瀟湘館中來。此時黛玉已好了大半了，見香菱也進園來住，自是喜歡。香菱因笑道：「我這一進來了，也得空兒，好歹教我做詩，就是我的造化了！」黛玉笑道：「既要學做詩，你就拜我為師。我雖不通，大略也還教的起你。」香菱笑道：「果然這樣，我就拜你為師，你可不許厭煩的。」黛玉道：「什麼難事，也值得去學？不過是起承轉合。當中承轉，是兩副對子：平聲的對仄聲；虛的對實的，實的對虛的。若是果有了奇句，連平仄虛實不對都使的的。」

香菱笑道：「怪道我常弄本舊詩偷兒看一兩首，又有對的極工的，又有不對的；又聽見說，『一三五不論，二四六分明，』看古人的詩上，亦有順的，亦有二四六上錯的：所以天天疑惑。如今聽你一說，原來這些規矩竟是沒事的，只要詞句新奇為上。」黛玉道：「正是這個道理。詞句究竟還是末事，第一是立意要緊。若意趣真了，連詞句不用修飾，自是好的：這叫做『不為辭害意』。」

香菱道：「我只愛陸放翁的『重簾不卷留香久，古硯微凹聚墨多』，說的真切有趣！」黛玉道：「你們因不知詩，所以見了這淺近的就愛。一入了這個格局，再學不出來的。你只聽我說：你若真心要學，我這裡有《王摩詰全集》，你且把他的五言律一百首細心揣摩透熟了，然後再讀一百二十首老杜的七言律，次之再李青蓮的七言絕句讀一二百首。肚子裡先有了這三個人做了底子，然後再陶淵明、應、劉、謝、阮、庾、鮑等人的一看。你又是這樣一個極聰明伶俐的人，不用一年工夫，不愁不是詩翁了！」香菱聽了，笑道：「既這樣，好姑娘，你就這書給我出來，我帶回去，夜裡念幾首也是好的。」黛玉聽說，便命紫鵑將王右丞的五言律拿來，遞與香菱，道：「你只看有紅圈的，都是我選的，有一首念一首。不明白的，問你姑娘；或者遇見我，我講與你就是了。」

香菱拿了詩，回至蘅蕪院中，諸事不管，只向燈下一首一首的讀起來。寶釵連催他數次睡覺，他也不睡。寶釵見他這般苦心，只得隨他去了。

一日，黛玉方梳洗完了，只見香菱吟吟的送了書來，又要換杜律。黛玉笑道：「共記得多少首？」香菱笑道：「凡紅圈選的，我盡讀了。」黛玉道：「可領略了些沒有？」香菱笑道：「我倒領略了些，只不知不是，說給你聽聽。」

He didn't, however, drag him down and strike him with a rattan or cane, but recklessly assaulted him, while he stood before him, with something or other, which he laid hold of, and broke his face open in two places. We understand that Mrs. Hsüeh has in here some medicine or other for applying on wounds, so do try, miss, and find a ball of it and let me have it!"

Hearing this, Pao-ch'ai speedily directed Ying Erh to go and look for some, and, on discovering two balls of it, she brought them over and handed them to P'ing Erh.

"Such being the case," Pao-ch'ai said, "do make, on your return, the usual inquiries for me, and I won't then need to go."

P'ing Erh turned towards Pao-ch'ai, and expressed her readiness to execute her commission, after which she betook herself home, where we will leave her without further notice.

After Hsiang Ling, for we will take up the thread of our narrative with her, completed her visits to the various inmates, she had her evening meal. Then when Pao-ch'ai and every one else went to dowager lady Chia's quarters, she came into the Hsiao Hsiang lodge. By this time Tai-yü had got considerably better. Upon hearing that Hsiang Ling had also moved into the garden, she, needless to say, was filled with delight.

"Now, that I've come in here," Hsiang Ling then smiled and said, "do please teach me, at your leisure, how to write verses. It will be a bit of good luck for me if you do."

"Since you're anxious to learn how to versify," Tai-yü answered with a smile, "you'd better acknowledge me as your tutor; for though I'm not a good hand at poetry, yet I know, after all, enough to be able to teach you."

"Of course you do!" Hsiang Ling laughingly remarked. "I'll readily treat you as my tutor. But you mustn't put yourself to any trouble!"

"Is there anything so difficult about this," Tai-yü pursued, "as to make it necessary to go in for any study? Why, it's purely and simply a matter of openings, elucidations, embellishments and conclusions. The elucidations and embellishments, which come in the centre, should form two antithetical sentences, the even tones must pair with the uneven. Empty words must correspond with full words; and full words with empty words. In the event of any out-of-the-way lines, it won't matter if the even and uneven tones, and the empty and full words do not pair."

"Strange though it may appear," smiled Hsiang Ling, "I often handle books with old poems, and read one or two stanzas, whenever I can steal the time; and some among these I find pair most skilfully, while others don't. I have also heard that the first, third and fifth lines are of no consequence; and that the second, fourth and sixth must be clearly distinguished. But I notice that there are in the poetical works of ancient writers both those which accord with the rules, as well as those whose second, fourth and sixth lines are not in compliance with any rule. Hence it is that my mind has daily been full of doubts. But after the hints you've given me, I really see that all these formulas are of no account, and that the main requirement is originality of diction."

"Yes, that's just the principle that holds good," Tai-yü answered. "But diction is, after all, a last consideration. The first and foremost thing is the choice of proper sentiments; for when the sentiments are correct, there'll even be no need to polish the diction; it's certain to be elegant. This is called versifying without letting the diction affect the sentiments."

"What I admire," Hsiang Ling proceeded with a smile; "are the lines by old Lu Fang;

"The double portière, when not raised, retains the fragrance long.
An old inkslab, with a slight hole, collects plenty of ink.

"Their language is so clear that it's charming."

"You must on no account," Tai-yü observed, "read poetry of the kind. It's because you people don't know what verses mean that you, no sooner read any shallow lines like these, than they take your fancy. But when once you get into this sort of style, it's impossible to get out of it. Mark my words! If you are in earnest about learning, I've got here Wang Mo-chieh's complete collection; so you'd better take his one hundred stanzas, written in the pentameter rule of versification, and carefully study them, until you apprehend them thoroughly. Afterwards, look over the one hundred and twenty stanzas of Lao T'u, in the heptameter rule; and next read a hundred or two hundred of the heptameter four-lined stanzas by Li Ch'ing-lieu. When you have, as a first step, digested these three authors, and made them your foundation, you can take T'ao Yuan-ming, Ying, Liu, Hsieh, Yüan, Yü, Pao and other writers and go through them once. And with those sharp and quick wits of yours, I've no doubt but that you will become a regular poet before a year's time."

"Well, in that case," Hsiang Ling smiled, after listening to her, "bring me the book, my dear miss, so that I may take it along. It will be a good thing if I can manage to read several stanzas at night."

At these words, Tai-yü bade Tzu Chüan fetch Wang Tso-ch'eng's pentameter stanzas. When brought, she handed them to Hsiang Ling. "Only peruse those marked with red circles" she said. "They've all been selected by me. Read each one of them; and should there be any you can't fathom, ask your miss about them. Or when you come across me, I can explain them to you."

Hsiang Ling took the poems and repaired back to the Heng Wu-yüan. And without worrying her mind about anything she approached the lamp and began to con stanza after stanza. Pao-ch'ai pressed her, several consecutive times, to go to bed; but as even rest was far from her thoughts, Pao-ch'ai let her, when she perceived what trouble she was taking over her task, have her own way in the matter.

Tai-yü had one day just finished combing her hair and performing her ablutions, when she espied Hsiang Ling come with smiles playing about her lips, to return her the book and to ask her to let her have T'u's poetical compositions in exchange.

"Of all these, how many stanzas can you recollect?" Tai-yü asked, smiling.

"I've read every one of those marked with a red circle," Hsiang Ling laughingly rejoined.

"Have you caught the ideas of any of them, yes or no?" Tai-yü inquired.

"Yes, I've caught some!" Hsiang Ling smiled. "But whether rightly or not I don't know. Let me tell you."

They used the backs of boards and sticks, and while he was standing there, I do not know what object was used to beat him, but his face was cut in two places. We heard that the <term>Yitaitai</term> <gloss>Aunt; specifically Aunt Xue</gloss> here has a certain medicine for treating staff wounds. Would you find a pill for me, Miss?

When Baochai heard this, she quickly ordered Ying’er to find two pills and give them to Ping’er. Baochai said: Since that is the case, go and give him my regards on my behalf; I will not go myself. Ping’er gave her word to Baochai and departed. This matter needs no further discussion.

Now, after Xiangling had met everyone and finished her evening meal, Baochai and the others went to Madam Wang’s quarters, while Xiangling herself came to the <term>Xiaoxiang Guan</term> <gloss>Naiad’s House; the residence of Lin Daiyu</gloss>. By this time, Daiyu was more than half recovered. Seeing that Xiangling had also come into the garden to live, she was naturally pleased. Xiangling said with a smile: Now that I have come in, I finally have some free time. If you would only teach me how to compose poetry, it would be my great good fortune!

Daiyu smiled and said: Since you want to learn to write poetry, you must take me as your master. Although I am not truly proficient, I can generally manage to teach you.

Xiangling laughed: If that is truly so, I shall take you as my master. You must not grow weary of me.

Daiyu said: What difficulty is there in it that makes it worth such fuss to learn? It is nothing more than <term>Qi, Cheng, Zhuan, He</term> <gloss>Introduction, Elucidation, Transition, and Conclusion; the four structural movements of a classical poem</gloss>. In the middle, the Elucidation and Transition are two pairs of couplets: level tones against deflected tones, empty words against solid words, and solid words against empty words. If one truly possesses a startling line, one may even ignore the rules of tonal balance and word-class correspondence.

Xiangling laughed: No wonder I often used to steal a look at one or two poems in old books, and some had perfect parallelism while others did not. I also heard people say, "the first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct." Looking at the poems of the ancients, some follow this and some are wrong on the second, fourth, or sixth syllables. I have been confused every day. Now that I hear you speak, it turns out these rules are actually of no consequence, provided that the language is novel and original.

Daiyu said: That is exactly the principle. Language and phrasing are, after all, secondary matters; the most important thing is the <term>Liyi</term> <gloss>The conception or intent of the poem</gloss>. If the intent and charm are genuine, the poem will be good even without polishing the words. This is called "not letting the phrasing harm the meaning."

Xiangling said: I only love <term>Lu Fangweng</term>’s <note>The Southern Song dynasty poet Lu You</note> lines: "The heavy curtains remain unrolled to keep the fragrance long; the ancient ink-slab is slightly concave where much ink gathers." It is so vivid and interesting!

Daiyu said: Because you do not yet know poetry, you love what is shallow and accessible. Once you enter that pattern, you will never be able to break out of it. Just listen to me: if you truly wish to learn, I have here the <term>Complete Works of Wang Mojie</term> <note>The Tang dynasty poet-painter Wang Wei</note>. First, take one hundred of his five-character regulated verses and contemplate them until you know them thoroughly. Then, read one hundred and twenty of <term>Old Du</term>’s <note>The poet Du Fu</note> seven-character regulated poems. Next, read one or two hundred of <term>Li Qinglian</term>’s <note>The poet Li Bai</note> seven-character quatrains. With these three men as your foundation, you can then look at the works of <term>Tao Yuanming</term>, <term>Ying Yang</term>, <term>Liu Zhen</term>, <term>Xie Lingyun</term>, <term>Ruan Ji</term>, <term>Yu Xin</term>, and <term>Bao Zhao</term>. Being such an exceptionally clever and sharp person, in less than a year’s work, you need not worry about not becoming a venerable poet!

Hearing this, Xiangling smiled: Since that is so, good Miss, please bring that book out for me. I will take it back and read a few poems at night.

Upon hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijuan to fetch the five-character regulated poems of <term>Wang Youcheng</term> <note>Another name for Wang Wei</note> and handed them to Xiangling, saying: Just look at the ones marked with red circles; those are the ones I have selected. Read them one by one. If there is anything you do not understand, ask your mistress <note>Baochai</note>, or if you run into me, I will explain it to you.

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the <term>Hengwu Yuan</term> <gloss>Alkaid Court; the residence of Xue Baochai</gloss>. Ignoring all other affairs, she simply began to read them one by one under the lamp. Baochai urged her several times to go to sleep, but she would not. Seeing her such devotion, Baochai had no choice but to let her be.

One day, just as Daiyu had finished washing and dressing, she saw Xiangling approaching with a beaming face to return the book and ask for the poems of Du Fu. Daiyu smiled: How many do you remember?

Xiangling laughed: All those selected with red circles, I have read them all.

Daiyu asked: Have you gained any insight into them?

Xiangling laughed: I have indeed gained some insight, but I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell it to you.

<summary>Xiangling begins her poetic apprenticeship under Lin Daiyu's tutelage in the Prospect Garden. Daiyu outlines a rigorous curriculum of Tang dynasty masters and explains that emotional sincerity is more important than technical rules.</summary>
<keywords>Xiangling, Lin Daiyu, poetry education, Wang Wei, Du Fu, Li Bai, Prospect Garden, literary theory, classical Chinese poetry</keywords>

He used the wrong end of the boards and rods, and while standing over him, I do not know what object he grabbed, but he gave him a beating and cut his face in two places. We heard that her Ladyship <note>Aunt Xue</note> here has a type of medicine for rod-wounds; would you find a pill for me, Miss?"

When Baochai heard this, she quickly ordered Ying'er to find two pills to give to Ping'er. Baochai said, "Since that is the case, go and give him my regards; I shall not go myself." Ping'er assented to Baochai and departed. This matter requires no further words.

Now it is said that after Xiangling had met everyone and finished her evening meal, Baochai and the others went to Madam Wang's quarters. Xiangling herself came to the <term>Xiaoxiang Guan</term> <gloss>Naiad's House, the residence of Lin Daiyu</gloss>. By this time, Daiyu was mostly recovered. Seeing Xiangling coming into the garden to live, she was naturally pleased. Xiangling laughed and said, "Now that I have come in, I shall have some spare time. If you would only teach me how to compose poetry, it would be my great good fortune!"

Daiyu smiled and said, "Since you want to learn poetry, you must take me as your master. Although I am not an expert, I am capable of teaching you the basics." Xiangling laughed, "If that is truly the case, I shall take you as my master. You must not find me annoying."

Daiyu said, "What is so difficult about it that it should be a burden to learn? It is nothing more than the <term>Qi Cheng Zhuan He</term> <gloss>the four steps of a poem: introduction, development, transition, and conclusion</gloss>. In the middle sections of development and transition, there are two pairs of couplets: level tones against oblique tones, empty words against solid words, and solid against empty. If you truly have a remarkable line, you can even disregard the rules of tones and structure."

Xiangling laughed, "No wonder I often steal a look at one or two poems in old books; some are perfectly matched, while others are not. I have also heard it said, 'The first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Looking at the poems of the ancients, some follow this and some are wrong in the second, fourth, and sixth positions. I was confused every day. Now hearing you speak, it turns out these rules do not matter at all, as long as the wording is novel and extraordinary."

Daiyu said, "That is exactly the principle. The wording is ultimately a secondary matter; the most important thing is the <term>Liyi</term> <gloss>the initial conception or intent</gloss>. If the intent and interest are genuine, the poem will be good even without polishing the words. This is called 'not letting the words harm the meaning.'"

Xiangling said, "I only love <term>Lu Fangweng</term> <gloss>the poet Lu You</gloss> and his lines: 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, keeping the fragrance long; the ancient inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It is so vivid and interesting!"

Daiyu said, "Because you do not know poetry, you love what is shallow and accessible. Once you fall into that pattern, you will never be able to learn your way out. Just listen to me: if you truly want to learn, I have the <term>Wang Mo-jie Quanji</term> <gloss>Complete Works of Wang Wei</gloss> here. Take his one hundred five-character regulated poems and study them until you have thoroughly grasped and mastered them. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>the poet Du Fu</note> seven-character regulated poems, followed by one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>the poet Li Bai</note> seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three men in your belly as a foundation, then look at the works of Tao Yuanming, Ying Yang, Liu Zhen, Xie Lingyun, Ruan Ji, Yu Xin, and Bao Zhao. Since you are such an extremely clever and bright person, in less than a year’s labor, you need not worry about not becoming a master poet!"

Hearing this, Xiangling laughed, "In that case, good Miss, please bring the book out for me. I will take it back and read a few poems at night." Upon hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijuan to bring the five-character regulated poems of <term>Wang Youcheng</term> <gloss>Wang Wei</gloss> and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Just look at those with red circles; I selected those myself. Read them one by one. If there is something you do not understand, ask your mistress <note>Baochai</note>, or if you meet me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the <term>Hengwu Yuan</term> <gloss>Enclosure of Fragrant Herbs, the residence of Xue Baochai</gloss>. Ignoring all other affairs, she began to read them one by one under the lamp. Baochai urged her to sleep several times, but she would not. Seeing her such painstaking devotion, Baochai had to let her be.

One day, just as Daiyu had finished washing and dressing, she saw Xiangling approaching with a beaming face to return the book and ask for the poems of Du Fu. Daiyu smiled and asked, "How many poems do you remember in total?" Xiangling laughed, "I have read all of those marked with red circles." Daiyu asked, "Have you gained any understanding?" Xiangling laughed, "I have indeed grasped something, though I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell it to you."

<note>clarification: He</note> used the boards and clubs backwards, and even while standing <note>clarification: she</note> did not know what object he grabbed, but he gave <note>clarification: her</note> a beating, and two places on her face were broken open. We heard that you, Madam <note>original: "姨太太" (yitaitai)</note>, have a kind of medicine here for application to club-wounds; would the Young Mistress <note>clarification: Baochai</note> find a pill to give me?"

Baochai heard this and hurried her maid Oriole <note>original: "鶯兒" (Yinger)</note> to go find two pills and give them to Pinger. Baochai said: "Since it is like this, go and give her my greetings; I shall not go myself." Pinger answered Baochai and left. No more need be said of this.

It is said that after Xiangling met everyone and ate the evening meal, Baochai and the others all went to Lady Wang's <note>clarification: Aunt Wang's</note> place. Xiangling went by herself to the潇湘館 <term>Xiaoxiang Guan</term> <gloss>Naiad's House</gloss>. At this time Daiyu was more than half recovered. Seeing that Xiangling had also come into the garden to live, she was naturally happy. Xiangling said with a smile: "Now that I have come in, I have some free time. If you would teach me to compose poetry, it would be my great good fortune!" Daiyu smiled and said: "Since you want to learn to compose poetry, you must take me as your master. Although I am not fully proficient, I can generally manage to teach you." Xiangling smiled: "If it is truly so, I shall take you as my master; you must not get tired of me." Daiyu said: "What is so difficult about it that it is worth such concern? It is no more than the opening, the development, the transition, and the conclusion <note>original: "起承轉合" (qi cheng zhuan he)</note>. Within the development and transition, there are two pairs of couplets: level tones against oblique tones, empty words against solid words, and solid words against empty words. If one truly has a miraculous line, it is permissible even if the tones and categories do not match."

Xiangling smiled: "No wonder I often take an old book of poems to steal a look at a few, and find some are perfectly matched while others are not. I have also heard it said, 'The first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Looking at the poems of the ancients, some follow this and some are wrong on the second, fourth, and sixth. I have been in doubt every day. Now hearing you speak, it turns out these rules are actually of no consequence, as long as the phrasing is novel and extraordinary." Daiyu said: "That is exactly the principle. Phrasing is, after all, a secondary matter; first and foremost, the 'conception' <note>original: "立意" (li yi)</note> is vital. If the intent and interest are genuine, then the poem is naturally good even without polished phrasing. This is called 'not letting the words damage the intent' <note>original: "不為辭害意" (bu wei ci hai yi)</note>."

Xiangling said: "I only love Lu Fangweng's <note>context: Lu You (1125–1210), a famous Southern Song dynasty poet</note> 'Heavy curtains unrolled keep the fragrance long; an old inkstone slightly concave gathers much ink.' It is described so vividly and interestingly!" Daiyu said: "Because you do not know poetry, you see these shallow and accessible lines and love them. Once you enter that pattern, you will never be able to learn your way out. Just listen to me: if you truly want to learn, I have the *Complete Works of Wang Mojie* <note>context: Wang Wei (699–759), a Tang dynasty poet and painter</note> here. You should first carefully study and master one hundred of his five-character regulated poems. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>context: Du Fu (712–770), the "Poet Sage" of the Tang dynasty</note> seven-character regulated poems. Next, read one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>context: Li Bai (701–762), the "Poet Immortal" of the Tang dynasty</note> seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three people as a foundation in your belly, then take a look at Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, Bao, and the others. You are such an extremely clever and sharp person; in less than a year's work, you need not worry about not being a master poet!" Hearing this, Xiangling smiled: "In that case, good Miss, take that book out for me, and I will take it back to read a few poems at night." Hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijuan to bring the five-character regulated poems of Wang the Right Vice-President <note>context: An official title for Wang Wei</note> and handed them to Xiangling, saying: "Only look at those with red circles; those are the ones I have selected. Read them one by one. If there is anything you do not understand, ask your mistress <note>clarification: Baochai</note>; or if you meet me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the 蘅蕪院 <term>Hengwu Yuan</term> <gloss>Alcaic Enclosure</gloss>. She ignored everything else and simply began to read them one by one under the lamp. Baochai urged her several times to go to sleep, but she would not. Seeing her such painstaking dedication, Baochai could only let her be.

One day, just as Daiyu had finished washing and combing, she saw Xiangling beaming as she brought the book back, wanting to exchange it for the poems of Du <note>clarification: Du Fu</note>. Daiyu smiled: "How many poems do you remember in total?" Xiangling smiled: "I have read all of those selected with red circles." Daiyu said: "Have you grasped some of the meaning?" Xiangling smiled: "I have indeed grasped some, but I do not know if I am right. Let me tell you about it."

<keywords>Xiangling, Lin Daiyu, Xue Baochai, poetry composition, Wang Wei, Du Fu, Li Bai, literary education, Xiaoxiang Guan, Hengwu Yuan</keywords>

...using the reverse side of boards and sticks, and while standing, he took something and beat him, breaking the skin on his face in two places. We heard that your mother has a kind of medicine here for staff wounds; please find a pill for me, Miss."

Upon hearing this, Baochai hurriedly ordered Ying'er to find two pills for Ping'er. Baochai said, "Since this is the case, go and give him my regards; I will not go myself." Ping'er answered Baochai and departed. This needs no further mention.

Now it is said that after Xiangling had met everyone and finished her evening meal, and while Baochai and the others went to Madam Wang's <note>clarification: the text refers to her as "Aunt," the mother of Baochai</note> quarters, she went alone to the Bamboo Lodge <note>original: "瀟湘館" (Xiaoxiang Guan)</note>. At this time, Daiyu was mostly recovered. Seeing that Xiangling had also entered the garden to live, she was naturally pleased. Xiangling said with a smile, "Now that I have come in and have some free time, if you would teach me how to compose poetry, it would be my great good fortune!" Daiyu smiled and said, "If you want to learn to write poetry, you must take me as your teacher. Although I am not truly proficient, I can generally manage to teach you." Xiangling laughed, "If that is really so, I shall take you as my teacher, and you must not grow weary of me." Daiyu said, "What is so difficult about it that it is worth such concern? It is nothing more than the introduction, development, transition, and conclusion <note>original: "起承轉合" (qi cheng zhuan he)</note>. Within the development and transition, there are two pairs of couplets: level tones against oblique tones, and empty words against solid words, or solid against empty. If you truly have a remarkable line, it is acceptable even if the tones and the balance of words do not match perfectly."

Xiangling laughed, "No wonder when I used to secretly look at one or two poems in an old book, some were perfectly balanced while others were not. I also heard people say, 'the first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Looking at the poems of the ancients, some followed this while others were wrong on the second, fourth, or sixth syllables. I was confused every day. Now hearing you speak, it seems these rules are actually of no consequence, as long as the phrasing is novel and original." Daiyu said, "That is exactly the principle. Phrasing is ultimately a secondary matter; the most important thing is the conception <note>original: "立意" (liyi)</note>. If the intent and interest are genuine, the poem will be good even without polishing the words. This is what is called 'not letting the words damage the meaning'."

Xiangling said, "I only love Lu Fangweng's <note>context: the Southern Song dynasty poet Lu You</note> lines: 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, keeping the fragrance long; the ancient ink-slab is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It is so vivid and interesting!" Daiyu said, "Because you do not understand poetry, you love what is shallow and accessible. Once you enter that pattern, you will never be able to break out of it. Listen to me: if you truly want to learn, I have the *Complete Works of Wang Mojie* <note>context: the Tang dynasty poet Wang Wei</note> here. Take a hundred of his five-syllable regulated poems and study them until you have mastered them thoroughly. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>context: the poet Du Fu</note> seven-syllable regulated poems, and after that, one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>context: the poet Li Bai</note> seven-syllable quatrains. Once you have these three people as a foundation in your mind, you can then look at Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, Bao, and the others. Since you are such an intelligent and clever person, in less than a year's time, you need not worry about becoming a true poet!" Hearing this, Xiangling smiled, "If that is so, good Miss, please bring that book out for me. I will take it back and it will be good to read a few poems at night." Hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijuan to bring the five-syllable regulated poems of Wang the Right Chancellor <note>context: another title for Wang Wei</note> and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Only look at those with red circles; those are the ones I have selected. Read them one by one. If there is something you do not understand, ask your mistress <note>clarification: Baochai</note>, or if you run into me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the Garden of Plantain Marvels <note>original: "蘅蕪院" (Hengwu Yuan)</note>. Neglecting all other matters, she began to read poem after poem under the lamp. Baochai urged her several times to go to sleep, but she would not. Seeing her such heart-felt devotion, Baochai had to let her be.

One day, just as Daiyu had finished washing and dressing, she saw Xiangling coming in with a beaming face to return the book, asking to exchange it for the poems of Du Fu. Daiyu smiled and asked, "How many do you remember?" Xiangling laughed, "I have read all of those marked with red circles." Daiyu asked, "Have you gained any understanding of them?" Xiangling smiled and said, "I have indeed gained some understanding, but I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell it to you."

[context] But he had particularly cultivated logic, and was profoundly skilled in the interpretation of the holy Scriptures;
insomuch that the heretic Eunomius often shrank from the acumen which his reasoning displayed. As regards his diet he was not simple; for although he practised the strictest moderation, yet his table was always sumptuously furnished. He was also accustomed to indulge himself by wearing white garments, and bathing twice a day in the public baths. And when some one asked him 'why he, a bishop, bathed himself twice a day?' he replied, 'Because it is inconvenient to bathe thrice.' Going one day from courtesy to visit the bishop Arsacius, he was asked by one of the friends of that bishop, 'why he wore a garment so unsuitable for a bishop? And where it was written that an ecclesiastic should be clothed in white?' 'Do you tell me first,' said he, 'where it is written that a bishop should wear black?' When he that made the inquiry knew not what to reply to this counter-question: 'You cannot show,' rejoined Sisinnius, 'that a priest should be clothed in black. But Solomon is my authority, whose exhortation is, Let your garments be white.
And our Saviour in the Gospels appears clothed in white raiment: moreover he showed Moses and Elias to the apostles, clad in white garments.' His prompt reply to these and other questions called forth the admiration of those present. Again when Leontius bishop of Ancyra in Galatia Minor, who had taken away a church from the Novatians, was on a visit to Constantinople, Sisinnius went to him, and begged him to restore the church. But he received him rudely, saying, 'You Novatians ought not to have churches; for you take away repentance, and shut out Divine mercy.' As Leontius gave utterance to these and many other such revilings against the Novatians, Sisinnius replied: 'No one repents more heartily than I do.' And when Leontius asked him 'Why do you repent?' 'That I came to see you,' said he. On one occasion John the bishop having a contest with him, said, 'The city cannot have two bishops.' 'Nor has it,' said Sisinnius. John being irritated at this response, said, 'You see you pretend that you alone are the bishop.' 'I do not say that,' rejoined Sisinnius; 'but that I am not bishop in your estimation only, who am such to others.' John being still more chafed at this reply, said, 'I will stop your preaching; for you are a heretic.' To which Sisinnius good-humoredly replied, 'I will give you a reward, if you will relieve me from so arduous a duty.' John being softened a little by this answer, said, 'I will not make you cease to preach, if you find speaking so troublesome.' So facetious was Sisinnius, and so ready at repartee: but it would be tedious to dwell further on his witticisms. Wherefore by means of a few specimens we have illustrated what sort of a person he was, deeming these as sufficient. I will merely add that he was celebrated for erudition, and on account of it all the bishops who succeeded him loved and honored him; and not only they but all the leading members of the senate also esteemed and admired him. He is the author of many works: but they are characterized by too great an affectation of elegance of diction, and a lavish intermingling of poetic expressions. On which account he was more admired as a speaker than as a writer; for there was dignity in his countenance and voice, as well as in his form and aspect, and every movement of his person was graceful. On account of these features he was loved by all the sects, and he was in special favor with Atticus the bishop. But I must conclude this brief notice of Sisinnius.
Not long after the death of John, the Emperor Arcadius died also.

# SOCRATES SCHOLASTICUS BOOK 6

<meta>This page continues the description of Sisinnius, the Novatian bishop of Constantinople.</meta>

it was often his habit to avoid his own skill in debate. In his manner of life he was not simple, yet he practiced this expense with extreme self-control. He lived luxuriously, wearing white garments and bathing twice each day in the public baths. Once, when someone asked him why he, being a bishop, would bathe twice a day, he replied: Because I cannot manage a third time. On another occasion, while visiting the bishop Sergius, he was asked by one of Arsacius’s followers why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a priest should dress in white. He said: You tell me first where it is written that a bishop must wear black garments. When the questioner was at a loss for an answer, Sisinnius followed up his counter-question: You would not be able to show that a priest must dress in black. But Solomon advised me, saying, Let your garments be white <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels is shown wearing white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah to the apostles dressed in white. By saying these and many other things readily, he was greatly admired by those present. 

When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, took away a church from the Novatians, Sisinnius went to him while he was staying in Constantinople and asked him to return the church. Leontius answered warmly and said to him: You Novatians ought not to have churches, for you do away with repentance <note>The Novatians held a rigorist view that those who fell away during persecution could not be readmitted to the church</note> and shut out the loving-kindness of God. When Leontius had said these and many other such harsh things against the Novatians, Sisinnius said: Truly, no one has ever repented as much as I have. When the other asked again how he had repented, Sisinnius replied: Because I saw you. 

Once, when John <note>John Chrysostom, the Bishop of Constantinople</note> was finding fault with him and saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said: Indeed, it does not have two. When John became angry and said: You see that you alone are a bishop by your own will, Sisinnius replied: I do not say this, but rather that I am not a bishop in your eyes, though I am one in the ears of the people. John, becoming indignant at what was said, replied: I will stop you from preaching, for you are a heretic. To this Sisinnius replied gracefully: I would even give you a reward if you would relieve me of such great labor. John, softened at once by this answer, said: I will not stop your freedom of speech if speaking is a burden to you. 

Such was the readiness and grace of Sisinnius in his replies. To write and record all his sayings would be a long task. I have shown through a few examples what kind of man he was when he took up leadership. [context] For as diseases arising from depraved meat and drink, from Animals, Vegetables, and fruites of the Earth; with Arcanums of Herbs and Roots are healed; so if from Mettals and Minerals, with their Arcanums also, in such Arcanums of Vegetables are refused. In the same manner
plainly, the greatest part of diseases, coming from Celestial Influence, and from the Astral Impression of the greater and lesser Worlds firmament, admit not of cure with promiscuous Remedies, as by Arcanums of Herbs, Minerals, and Metalls, but by Astronomick Influence, the cure is instituted with such things only as have an Analogy to the greater and lesser World, in which is the true Magnetick force of the Firmament, and a Celestial Impression of resisting diseases, caused by the Firmament of the greater and lesser World, as is apparent in Arsemart, the greater Comphry, Dragonwort, and the greater Wallwort. If supernaturally, the disease or dolour take its beginning from Inchantment or by Magical Impression of Ascendants, the endeavouring the Cure by the three former ways is fruitless and unprofitable; but according to Paracelsus, process must be made Magically and Supernaturally, and the evil by the same means it was inferr'd must again be expell'd. In the aforesaid Simples there is an Influential Attractive, and all according to Divine Ordination, Magically, Astronomically, and Magnetically cure; because in them is Medicine, and in Man the Magnet.
For as the Sun and Stars have power of attracting humidity from Inferiours, so Man (by the Magnetick attractive virtue placed in him, attracts Spirit instead of Nutriment, as a Loadstone draws Iron) and Inferiors have the same power of attracting from Superiors, as we see in time of the Pest; and these
[margin] ... Astral, Venenate, and Spiritual, the fift is such as are inflicted as a Scourge.
[margin] These Astral and Firmamental Infections are known by the ingenious Physician, and Firmamentally cured, for Art hath obtained a Medicine which impowers the Phy[s]itian ... to know and expell Firmamental diseases.
[margin] The Magnet of Man is Magical Cure, in which is a Celestial Impression after Contact of the Herb, the Herb until it be putrefied, attracts Medicine into the Ulcer, and so cures it.

There may be similarity in understanding without similarity in outward form. There may also be similarity in form without similarity in understanding. The Sage embraces similarity of understanding and pays no regard to similarity of form. The world in general is attracted by similarity of form, but remains indifferent to similarity of understanding. Those creatures that resemble them in shape they love and consort with; those that differ from them in shape they fear and keep at a distance. The creature that has a skeleton seven feet long, hands differently shaped from the feet, hair on its head, and an even set of teeth in its jaws, and walks erect, is called a man. But it does not follow that a man may not have the mind of a brute. Even though this be the case, other men will still recognise him as one of their own species in virtue of his outward form. Creatures which have wings on the back or horns on the head, serrated teeth or extensile talons, which fly overhead or run on all fours, are called birds and beasts. But it does not follow that a bird or a beast may not have the mind of a man. Yet, even if this be so, it is nevertheless assigned to another species because of the difference in form. P'ao Hsi, Nü Kua, Shen Nung and Hsia Hou had serpents' bodies, human faces, ox-heads and tigers' snouts. Thus, their forms were not human, yet their virtue was of the saintliest. Chieh of the Hsia dynasty, Chou of the Yin, Huan of the Lu State, and Mu of the Ch'u State, were in all external respects, as facial appearance and possession of the seven channels of sense, like unto other men; yet they had the minds of savage brutes. Howbeit, in seeking perfect wisdom, men attend to the outward form alone, which will not bring them near to it.

When the Yellow Emperor fought with Yen Ti on the field of P'an-ch'uan, his vanguard was composed of bears, wolves, panthers, lynxes and tigers, while his ensign-bearers were eagles, ospreys, falcons and kites. This was forcible impressment of animals into the service of man. The Emperor Yao entrusted K'uei with the regulation of music. When the latter tapped the musical stone in varying cadence, all the animals danced to the sound of the music. When the strains of the Shao were heard on the flute, the phoenix itself flew down to assist. This was the attraction of animals by the power of music.
